title: U . S . sizzles under wilting heat that may shift west this week
text:
A heat dome is searing down across the central U.S., focusing on the Great Plains, Midwest and Mississippi River Valley, including Memphis and St. Louis, driving up demand across regional power grids and leaving more than 100 million people sweltering.
Separately, in the Pacific, Hurricane Fausto is forecast to lose strength, passing north of the Hawaiian Islands as a tropical storm on Tuesday and Wednesday, while Hurricane Genevieve is intensifying off Mexico’s Baja California coast.
Extreme heat warnings and advisories cover the central U.S. from the North Dakota-Canada border south to Dallas. At least 20 daily high temperature records are set to be challenged or broken across the region on Sunday, with 33 warm overnight lows threatened as well, the U.S. Weather Prediction Center said.
The heat and humidity will make temperatures feel as scorching as 112 degrees Fahrenheit as the heat index rises across large parts of the central U.S., the National Weather Service said. In St. Louis, where Sunday’s high is forecast to hit 97 degrees, the moisture in the atmosphere could create a feels-like temperature closer to 116 degrees, and in Dallas a high of 102 degrees is expected, with a heat index as high as 109 degrees.
“A big heat dome is centered of the Rocky Mountains and Plains that’s going to bring record breaking temperatures,” said Alex DaSilva, a meteorologist with the commercial forecaster AccuWeather Inc. “Triple-digit heat is stretching from the Rockies to the Plains. There’s some dangerous heat there.”
At least 105 million people across the U.S. are under heat advisories or extreme heat warnings for Sunday, including in Southern California, the Weather Prediction Center said. As the weather sends people fleeing to air conditioners for relief, the Southwest Power Pool and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, which together cover at least parts of 20 states, have said that loads may rise. Stagnant air under the large high-pressure system may also crimp wind-generated power at peak times.
High temperatures can hurt some crops but benefit big retailers as sales of air conditioners and fans jump.
On top of the sweltering temperatures there’s a chance for severe thunderstorms, wind and hail at the edges, AccuWeather’s Alex DaSilva said. Saturday brought 89 filtered reports of high winds and two of large hailstorms, mainly in Montana and South Dakota, the U.S. Storm Prediction Center said.
The heat dome will continue to raise temperatures across the western and central U.S. this week before the focus shifts to the west by next weekend, said Bob Oravec, a senior branch forecaster at the Weather Prediction Center.
Heat across the Southwest and California is likely to last into the beginning of August, he said.
In the Pacific, the main impact from Fausto is likely to be rough surf and rip currents to the northern facing sides of the Hawaiian islands, said AccuWeather’s DaSilva. “Overall, I don’t think this will be a big deal for them.”
As Fausto fades, Hurricane Genevieve is intensifying off Mexico’s southwest coast, potentially on its way to becoming a Category 4 major storm, bringing rough seas to the southern parts of the Baja California peninsula, the National Hurricane Center said.
Genevieve is the eastern Pacific’s seventh storm, a mark typically reached by Aug. 11, showing the season that began on May 15 is slightly ahead of its normal pace.

title: High surf in Southern California : Waves as high as 10 feet affecting roughly 700 miles of coastline
text:
HUNTINGTON BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- Beachgoers heading to the Southern California coast this weekend are being urged to use caution as Hurricane Genevieve fuels large surf and dangerous rip currents along hundreds of miles of coastline.
Waves as high as 10 feet are affecting roughly 700 miles of the California coast, creating hazardous ocean conditions for swimmers and surfers.
Lifeguards are responding to hundreds of water rescues each day. In Los Angeles County, officials say every lifeguard on duty is averaging two to three water rescues per shift this week.
The dangerous surf comes as the U.S. Open of Surfing continues in Huntington Beach. The hazardous conditions are not limited to Orange County. Strong surf and dangerous rip currents are also expected at beaches in Los Angeles and Ventura counties.
Officials advise anyone caught in a rip current to swim parallel to the shoreline, then angle away from the current and head back toward shore.
Some beachgoers said the rough conditions are keeping them out of the water.
"I wouldn't go out there today, "Angie Chrisfield said. "Number 1, I am too old. Number 2, it's too rough out there."
Lifeguards are also reminding visitors to check in with beach personnel before entering the water, noting that ocean conditions can change quickly.

title: Genevieve becomes first Category 5 hurricane in East Pacific in two years
text:
Genevieve becomes first Category 5 hurricane in East Pacific in two years
Genevieve becomes the First Category 5 Hurricane since Kristy of 2024
Hurricane Genevieve reaches a Category 5 strength on early Monday, becoming the first one in the East Pacific region in two years as per recent forecast.
According to the National Hurricane Center in Miami, though Genevieve had maximum sustained winds of 160mph, it is not expected to make landfall and will stay far out to sea on a course parallel with the Mexico coast.
Speaking about the hurricane’s location, its center was located about 530 miles southwest of Manzanillo while heading toward northwest at 13 mph. Genevieve becomes the first Category 5 hurricane in the East Pacific since Kristy of 2024.
Right now no coastal watches and warnings have been issued but the hurricane center reported that swells generated by the storm which could trigger “life-threatening surf and rip current conditions”, were impacting parts of southwestern Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula.
As per reports, the storm will start to weaken from Tuesday.
In the northwest in the Pacific, the intensity of hurricane Fausto has weakened to Category 1 storm as it is moving towards the general direction of the Hawaiian Islands.
Despite the reduction in the intensity of the Fausto storm, the forecaster cautioned that it still poses a threat to parts of Hawaii. Currently, the system packs maximum sustained winds of 80 mph and is positioned approximately 670 miles east of Hilo.

title: Tropical Storm Fausto to splash Hawaii , Genevieve sends swells to Mexico
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Rough surf was possible for Hawaii and Mexico on Tuesday thanks to two tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean that forecasters said were sending strong waves to some coastal areas.
Tropical Storm Fausto was expected to pass just north of the Hawaiian islands starting Tuesday night, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Fausto had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was expected to weaken from tropical storm strength early Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Fausto was about 310 miles east-northeast of Honolulu and moving west-northwest near 12 mph. Forecasters said strong currents from the tropical storm could create dangerous conditions on some Hawaii beaches.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Genevieve strengthened to a Category 4, the hurricane center said. Maximum sustained winds were 130 mph for the major hurricane, which was about 590 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.
Swells from Genevieve were reaching Baja California and coastal southwestern Mexico. Forecasters warned of life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
On the forecast track, Genevieve was expected to fluctuate in intensity for about a day before consistently weakening.

title: Wednesday Weather | Fausto weakens as trade winds return
text:
HONOLULU (Island News) -- Tropical Depression Fausto is passing north of the Hawaiian Islands today and continues to weaken. While the storm is not expected to directly impact Hawaii, it will bring light winds, warm temperatures and muggy conditions across the state.
Most areas will start the day dry, with only a few showers over windward communities. As the day warms up, light sea breezes will help clouds build over island interiors, bringing the chance for a few afternoon showers. A brief heavy shower is possible in some spots, but widespread flooding is not expected.
By tonight, Fausto's remnants will move farther away, allowing breezy trade winds to return. More typical Hawaii weather is expected through the rest of the week, with showers mainly over windward and mountain areas. Humidity will also begin to decrease by Friday, making conditions feel more comfortable.
At the beaches, east shore surf will continue to come down today, although a High Surf Advisory remains in effect through this afternoon. South shore surf will increase slightly on Thursday, while east shore surf is expected to build again later this week as swells from Hurricane Genevieve arrive.

title: Pictures show Malibu beach destroyed by sudden coastal erosion
text:
Apocalyptic photos captured the latest blow to Malibu’s battered coastline after severe erosion left eight-foot drop-offs along the bluffs at iconic Point Dume Beach, forcing officials to shut down road access and warn the area had become too dangerous to enter.
The closure comes as the California Post reveals Malibu is still reeling from the aftermath of the Palisades Fire, with many homeowners already facing years of rebuilding and longstanding concerns over the stability of the coastline and Pacific Coast Highway.
Los Angeles County Department of Beaches and Harbors closed Westward Beach Road beyond the toll gate and the Point Dume Beach parking lot after overnight high tides and pounding surf carved away sections of the bluff, leaving “drop-offs approaching 8 feet in some locations,” KTLA reported.
“The bluff edge is unstable, with drop-offs approaching 8 feet in some locations, creating a significant safety hazard,” the department said in an advisory Sunday.
Beachfront homeowner Carl Randall, who is rebuilding after losing his home in the fire, told the California Post that erosion and the fragile bluff have complicated construction from the start.
“We can’t be too close to the edge or the edge will collapse,” Randall said, explaining why crews have had to work in an extremely narrow space between the ocean and traffic racing along PCH.
Randall said he had asked the city to move the highway farther inland to create more room for construction, but was granted only half the distance he requested. He also described the rebuilding process as a “battle,” requiring multiple engineering reviews and approvals unique to building along Malibu’s coastline.

The latest erosion is likely to heighten concerns for homeowners still weighing whether to rebuild or sell altogether. More than a year and a half after the Palisades Fire, only a fraction of destroyed beachfront homes have begun reconstruction, with many residents citing soaring construction costs, permitting hurdles and uncertainty over Malibu’s changing coastline.
Temporary chemical toilets and hand-washing stations have been installed after the erosion damaged a water line serving the public restrooms.
The dangerous conditions were fueled by powerful southerly swells generated by Hurricane Genevieve, which battered Southern California beaches this week with 5- to 7-foot waves, dangerous rip currents and coastal flooding.
The closures will remain in place until further notice as county crews assess the damage — the latest setback for a stretch of Malibu coastline where many residents are still struggling to rebuild after the Palisades Fire.

title: Extreme Weather North America Brings Alaska Snow Wisconsin Tornado and Hurricane Genevieve With Millions Under Alerts
text:
Such severe weather events are not typically seen in North America. Meanwhile, parts of the continent are being pounded by strong storms, unseasonal snowfall, tornado threats, and hurricane activity. Surprising snow in Alaska. Severe thunderstorms throughout the middle of the country. Hurricane watches on the coast. Millions of Americans are being asked to stay alert. Meteorologists are monitoring the rapidly changing conditions while municipalities brace for potential impacts.
Several Weather Systems Threaten Regions in North America
Extreme weather: North America at risk from all parts of the continent. Alaska is buried in unexpected snow, tornadoes threaten sections of Wisconsin, and coastal areas fear Hurricane Genevieve. Storms are being tracked by forecasters and warnings are being issued to help people prepare.
Climate Change Is Here with Unseasonal Snow in Alaska

Cold air will move into the area with wintry conditions over areas of the state impacting transportation and outdoor activities. Residents should check local forecasts, particularly in areas that could see slick roads or impaired visibility. Severe thunderstorms in Wisconsin bring a significant risk of tornado activity, as storm systems are bringing strong winds, heavy rain, and lightning to parts of many states under weather alerts. In the worst circumstances, individuals are encouraged to prepare for emergencies and stay off the roads unless they have to be out.

Mexico’s Pacific Coast With Heavy Rain and Wind

Emergency officials are going over evacuation preparations and are reminding individuals living in critical locations to take precautions in case of any fallout. Officials are urging residents along the shore to watch official updates and not to believe unfounded reports during the storm.
Millions Across North America Under Severe Weather Warnings

title: Hot temps , Saharan dust slap Florida , but when will tropics heat up ?
text:
More Saharan dust is moving across the Atlantic toward Florida, which is helping keep any tropical cyclones from developing.
That doesn't mean you should let your guard down. Forecasters still warn residents should be prepared, especially as we approach the busiest portion of the season.
In the Pacific, Hurricane Genevieve is slowly weakening July 28, while Tropical Storm Fausto is expected to pass north of the Hawaiian Island tonight, July 28-29, bringing "significant surf."
The next named storm in the Atlantic will be Cristobal. The third named storm in the Atlantic typically forms around Aug. 3, according to NOAA.

Heat continues to impact Florida July 28, with extreme heat warnings and heat advisories issued for millions across the Panhandle and peninsula.
Here's the latest advisory from the National Hurricane Center as of 2 p.m., July 28:
When is hurricane season in Florida?
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.
Ninety-seven percent of tropical cyclone activity occurs during this time period, NOAA said.
The Atlantic basin includes the northern Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean Sea and Gulf of America, as the Gulf of Mexico is now known in the U.S. per an order from President Trump. NOAA and the National Hurricane Center are now using Gulf of America on its maps and in its advisories.
Countdown clock to end of 2026 Atlantic hurricane season
Where is Hurricane Genevieve going?
Hurricane Genevieve is slowly weakening but remained a Category 3 storm as of the 8 a.m. PT advisory from the National Hurricane Center.
Maximum sustained winds are near 125 mph, with higher gusts. Steady weakening is forecast over the next several days.
- Location: 530 miles southwest of the southern tip of Baja California
- Maximum sustained winds: 125 mph
- Movement: west-northwest at 9 mph
Will Tropical Storm Fausto hit Hawaii?
Tropical Storm Fausto is expected to pass north of the Hawaiian Islands Tuesday night through late Wednesday, July 29.
Large surf and strong currents will lead to dangerous conditions.
- Location: 265 miles northeast of Hilo, Hawaii; 400 miles east of Honolulu
- Maximum sustained winds: 60 mph
- Movement: west at 14 mph
Saharan dust approaching Florida
"Another dust plume is expected to arrive in Florida at the very end of the week and into the weekend," according to Alex DaSilva, AccuWeather lead hurricane expert via email Aug. 27.
"The dust is expected to increase in concentration late this weekend into early next week.
"It is still common at the start of August for large amounts of Saharan dust to move all the way across the Atlantic and even into the United States. Hazy sunshine and enhanced sunsets will be possible with this dust. This dust will also help to keep the main development region quiet for at least 10 days."
National Hurricane Center tracking no disturbances, 3 tropical waves
There are no disturbances listed by the National Hurricane Center on its tropical outlook map as of 2 p.m. July 28, and no tropical cyclone activity is expected during the next seven days.
Forecasters are watching three tropical waves:
- A tropical wave is in the E Atlantic with axis near 36W, extending from 06N to 15N, and moving westward at around 17 to 23 mph.
- A tropical wave is over the E Caribbean with axis near 63.5W, extending from 10N to 19N, and moving westward at 17 to 23 mph.
- A tropical wave is in the SW Caribbean with axis along 83W, from 06N to 18N, and moving westward at around 11 to 17 mph.
What is a tropical wave?
"Tropical waves are clusters of showers and thunderstorms that act as the seedlings for many tropical storms throughout the Atlantic season," said Alex DaSilva, AccuWeather lead hurricane expert, via email.
"There are about 60 tropical waves that move across the Atlantic each year, and roughly 10 percent to 15 percent of them develop into a tropical system. That's about one in seven.
"Tropical waves are important because they contribute to about 80 percent of all major hurricanes."
How many tropical storms, hurricanes are in a typical season?
The 30-year average, from 1991 to 2020, is for 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.
Florida weather radar for July 28, 2026
Weather watches and warnings issued in Florida
Extreme heat warnings, heat advisories issued for much of Florida July 28
An extreme heat warning has been issued by the National Weather Service for 13 counties, and a heat advisory has been issued for 37 counties, covering more than half of the state.
Temperatures are expected to reach range between 94 and 100 across portions of the Panhandle and Big Bend. Hold on, because the heat index could hit 115, according to the National Weather Service Tallahassee.
Rain coming for some parts of Florida as cold front stalls
"A wet pattern is in store across northern Florida later this week," DaSilva said.
"Starting Wednesday (July 29) and lasting through at least Sunday (Aug. 2), a stalled cold front is expected to meander near the Panhandle.
"This front will produce daily downpours and localized flooding. While the western Panhandle is drought free, the eastern Panhandle is in desperate need of rainfall. Residents will want to use caution as beneficial rain can come at the risk of flash flooding.
"Some areas in the Panhandle can get 2-4 inches, locally 6 inches of rain. The flooding risk across portions of the Panhandle can be increased due to dry soil. This dry, hard soil can allow the water to run off instead of being absorbed right away."
When is the peak of hurricane season?
The peak of the season is Sept. 10, with the most activity happening between mid-August and mid-October, according to the Hurricane Center.

title: California lifeguards are rescuing thousands during high surf , heat waves this summer

California lifeguards are rescuing thousands during high surf, heat waves this summer
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   
As millions of visitors flocked to the coast for a reprieve from the heat, lifeguards across California have sprung into action, making thousands of rescues over the last few days, some of which have gone viral on social media.
In Los Angeles County, lifeguards performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues over the weekend, according to a social media post.
At Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz County, a lifeguard was captured on video dragging a boy out of the water in a harrowing rescue.
And in San Diego County, local news reports showed a teen was injured over the weekend attempting a dramatic jump off Sunset Cliffs, when he fell short of the water and smacked into the terrain below him before falling into the ocean.
“With a Heat Advisory continuing across the Southland and a Southern Hemisphere swell expected to keep surf elevated throughout the week, we encourage everyone to take proper precaution,” Los Angeles County’s lifeguard division said on social media.
Hurricane Genevieve, which is whipping up the Pacific Ocean about 500 miles off the southern tip of Baja California, will send big waves rolling toward beaches this week, creating hazardous swimming conditions, the National Weather Service says.
Now a Category 4 hurricane and moving northwest with sustained winds of about 155 mph, Genevieve is expected to generate up to 11-foot swells by Wednesday afternoon along San Diego County beaches that face south and southwest.
In Orange County, waves could reach 10 feet at the Wedge in Newport Beach through Friday, according to a forecast from Surfline.
The hurricane will bring heavy surf and strong rip currents along L.A. County beaches, the National Weather Service says.
The summer has already been a busy one along the coast. Last month, lifeguards in Newport Beach rescued hundreds of swimmers during a weekend heat wave. It was during that heat wave that a 5-year-old girl was swept away farther south in Laguna Beach and drowned.
Temperatures are expected to stay warm through the week and dial up again into the weekend.
By Saturday, temperatures across the Southland will be 10 to 15 degrees above normal, according to the weather service. Forecasters expect the valleys to reach 100 to 110 degrees, the lower mountain and far interior areas to reach 105 to 112 degrees and the beaches to be in the 80s. More heat advisories will almost certainly be in place.
Times staff writer Ian James contributed to this report.

title: Worst of brutal SoCal heat wave is here : How long will it last ? How bad will it be ?
text:
Worst of brutal SoCal heat wave is here: How long will it last? How bad will it be?
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   
A major new heat wave will peak in Southern California over the next few days, bringing dangerous conditions and fire risk.
Here is what you need to know:
Timing
The heat wave begins Friday and will last through the weekend as a strong ridge of high pressure moves over the area.
“A big ridge of high pressure is associated with warmer temperatures,” said Carol Ciliberti, meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. “In this case it’s really high, so it’s giving us very hot conditions.”
Forecasters are calling for highs of 95 to 110 degrees in the valleys, with portions of the Antelope Valley potentially reaching 115 degrees, and 100 to 110 across the Inland Empire and high desert, with the low desert potentially nearing 120 degrees.
The coast will be a bit cooler, but still getting into the 80s.
Overnight temperatures won’t fall much below 70 degrees in many locations near Los Angeles, increasing the risk of heat stress.
Forecasters are calling for a slow cooling trend starting Sunday but warned that temperatures would still be above normal and remain that way for the foreseeable future as the high pressure persists.
Fire danger
The majority of Southern California, except for the immediate coastline, will see an enhanced risk of large wildfires Friday through Sunday, when conditions will be hottest and driest, said Kristen Stewart, meteorologist with the U.S. Forest Service.
Areas of particular concern include the foothills of the San Joaquin Valley and the region’s lower mountain areas, she said.
Beach conditions
Forecasters warned that those seeking to escape the heat with a trip to the beach should take care, as a large south swell from Hurricane Genevieve will continue to result in big waves. Southern California lifeguards reported performing thousands of rescues last weekend amid crowded conditions, rough surf and strong rip currents.
A high surf advisory is in effect through Saturday evening from San Diego County to Ventura County due to a large south swell from Tropical Cyclone Genevieve, with forecasters warning the risks are especially acute for south-facing beaches, including Manhattan Beach to Port Hueneme along the Malibu coast, and from Long Beach to the Palos Verdes Peninsula.
Many areas are seeing strong rip currents, and lifeguards have reported performing many rescues, Ciliberti said.
Health concerns
In addition to causing death and illness directly, extreme heat can exacerbate heart, lung and kidney disease, as well as mental health problems, experts said.
The heat wave was also expected to trigger a multiday smog event in some Los Angeles County regions, with the Air Quality Index potentially reaching unhealthy levels in Glendora and unhealthy levels for sensitive groups, including people with asthma, in the San Fernando, Santa Clarita and San Gabriel valleys, according to the South Coast Air Quality Management District. An ozone advisory was in effect from 10 a.m. Friday through 8 p.m. Sunday.
People can lessen the stress by staying inside somewhere that has air conditioning, taking the shadiest route possible when spending time outside, and submerging themselves in water — even if it’s just a cold foot bath.
People should also stay hydrated and refrain from leaving children or pets in vehicles. Those who must be outside are encouraged to wear lightweight, loose-fitting clothing and limit strenuous activities to the early morning or evening, he said.
Underlying drivers
Although forecasters said this heat wave will be drier than the last one, Southern California has seen a hot and unusually muggy summer, in part due to warm ocean temperatures.
Climate change from the burning of fossil fuels has resulted in hotter, more frequent heat waves, said David Eisenman, professor of medicine and co-director of the UCLA Center for Healthy Climate Solutions.
“Also, importantly, the nighttime doesn’t cool down like it used to, so our bodies are not able to recover in the same way,” he said.

title: Extreme heat and dangerous ocean rip currents about to hit San Diego County

A large high-pressure system will move into San Diego County late Wednesday, triggering several days of extreme heat that will coincide with potentially deadly rip currents along the coast, the National Weather Service says.
Lifeguards are concerned because the ocean is 3 to 7 degrees warmer than normal, which will draw larger numbers of people into the water at a time when Hurricane Genevieve is sending big waves and strong rip currents to local beaches.
The swell is expected to produce waves in the 5- to 7-foot range Thursday and Friday , with periodic sets reaching 9 to 11 feet, the weather service said. The biggest surf will occur at beaches that face south and southwest.

“San Diego Lifeguards will be fully staffed to inform and protect locals and visitors along our 17 miles of city coastline and Mission Bay,” San Diego Lifeguard Division Chief James Gartland said Tuesday.
“If you’re headed to the beach, please check in with a lifeguard, keep a close eye on the little ones and exercise caution when entering the water.”
Officials also are concerned about the effect that high temperatures could have on the public’s health, especially east of Interstate 15 where an extreme heat warning will go into effect 10 a.m. Friday and last until 8 p.m. on Sunday.
The weather service said that daytime highs in Ramona are expected to reach 93 on Wednesday, 95 on Thursday, 98 on Friday, 101 on Saturday and 100 on Sunday. The Borrego Springs area is forecast to be 113 on Wednesday, 115 on Thursday, 120 on Friday and Saturday, and 119 on Sunday. The highest temperature on record at Borrego Springs is 122, which might be tied this weekend.
Temperatures will be cooler at the coast, but still far above normal. San Diego is expected to hit 79 on Wednesday, 80 on Thursday, 82 on Friday, 85 on Saturday, and 83 on Sunday. The seasonal high is 76.

title: The Heat Advisory for inland areas ends this evening ; heat returns Friday
text:
Good Monday evening, Central Coast!
Below: Monday's official high temperatures. Cooler than average from San Luis Obispo to Santa Maria, down to Lompoc. Above average from Paso Robles to Santa Barbara.
Today marks the final day of the current heat advisory for San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties. A slight cooling trend is expected Tuesday and Wednesday as upper-level heights fall slightly. However, above-normal sea surface temperatures will maintain elevated humidity levels, particularly along the Santa Barbara County coast.
Heat Threat Returns Friday
Widespread heat risk looks to return Friday and continue through the weekend. The upper-level high pressure system currently centered over the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles will migrate westward beginning Thursday, initiating significant warming across both counties.
Near record high temperatures are possible Friday into the weekend.
Expected Temperature Ranges:
Interior valleys: up to 105 degrees
Coastal Valleys: above average high temperatures
Beaches may hit the upper 70s into the 80s
Overnight lows: warmer than average

Mountain and Forest Areas

Additional Hazards
Marine Conditions: A large south swell from Major Hurricane Genevieve continues to generate dangerous surf and high rip current risk along area beaches.

Surface flow will feature moderate to strong onshore flow during late afternoon hours. Morning low cloud patterns will remain consistent, though marine layer coverage may diminish during the peak heat period.

Below: The Heat Dome has been centered over the Texas Panhandle. We are on the back edge of the upper high, so the heat has been confined to the inland valleys.

title: Dangerous Conditions Persist Along SoCal Coast
text:
Officials continued to issue warnings about dangerous surf conditions Wednesday amid a heat wave that has sent droves of Southland residents to the seaside in search of a cool breeze.
The warnings come after Los Angeles County lifeguards announced that nearly 2,000 people were rescued from the ocean last weekend.
A large south swell from Hurricane Genevieve was sending large waves ashore while causing potentially deadly rip currents for some area beaches, according to the National Weather Service, which also cited Wednesday’s full moon as a factor in the powerful surf conditions.
The rip current risk was high on Wednesday, with wave heights between 5 and 7 feet in most areas, but as high as 9 feet at spots like Newport Beach in Orange County, according to the NWS, which issued the following advisories for area beaches:
— A high surf advisory from 5 p.m. Wednesday through 5 p.m. Saturday.
— A beach hazards statement through Saturday afternoon; and
— A coastal flood advisory Wednesday evening through 3 a.m. Saturday.
In addition to 1,950 ocean rescues, lifeguards also responded to 71,274 “preventative actions” and rendered medical aid to 517 people last weekend, prompting lifeguards to advise extreme caution.
“With a heat advisory continuing across the Southland and a southern hemisphere swell expected to keep surf elevated throughout the week, we encourage everyone to take proper precaution, and talk to a lifeguard about conditions before entering the water,” lifeguards advised on social media.
Officials in Malibu on Wednesday warned of an increased risk of drowning, especially for inexperienced swimmers.
“Rip currents can pull swimmers and surfers out to sea,” city officials warned. “Powerful waves can wash people off beaches and rocks and capsize small boats near shore. Other hazards include sneaker waves, beach erosion and debris in the water.”
Sneaker waves are large, powerful waves that seem to appear out of nowhere compared to the prevailing conditions.
Officials offered the following advice:
— Stay out of the water if possible;
— Enter the water near occupied Lifeguard towers;
— Check with Lifeguards about current ocean conditions before entering the water; and .
— Never let children play in or near the water without close adult supervision.

title: Bay Area set for return to hot weather , beaches dangerous
text:
A brief cool spell that sent temperatures below normal in the Bay Area is about to give way to conditions more common for late July, but the beach won’t be the safe retreat for relief that it might normally be.
The National Weather Service said temperatures will begin to elevate again on Monday, with the hottest inland areas such as Concord and Livermore forecast to move back into the low 90s. By the end of the week, the weather service anticipates temperatures will be above 95 degrees and threatening 100. In the Santa Clara Valley, the thermometer is expected to reach 90 by Friday.
Oakland is expected to be in the upper 70s all week, and San Francisco also is likely to see high temperatures in the 70s all week long.
All of that may drive people to consider a trip to the beach, but the weather service said that option could come with considerable danger this week.
“We have two hurricanes in the eastern Pacific Ocean. The remnants of one of them — Hurricane Fausto — has been sending some strong swells to us,” NWS meteorologist Anamaria Navarrete said. “The swells have been over five feet and that’s caused some of the waves to be breaking at 10-11 feet. We also have Hurricane Genevieve that’s still far from us, so given what we’ve seen with the swells so far, that will probably continue. The sneaker waves and the rip tides are all that much stronger.”
Those conditions were caught on video at a Santa Cruz beach Sunday, when life guards and good Samaritans helped to rescue a boy from powerful waves as they crashed over them.
A beach hazards statement issued by the weather service is in effect through Wednesday afternoon, though the weather service said that it’s possible it may last longer. Visitors at the beaches are expected to keep an eye on the waves and to stay off jetties, piers, rocks and other places where they might be vulnerable to the ocean’s pull.
The increasing temperatures come courtesy of the slight expansion of a heat dome that has enveloped much of the central and southern Plains, the southern Rockies, the Desert Southwest and the upper Midwest. In Death Valley, the high temperature forecast of 114 on Monday is expected to increase to 119 by Sunday.
A trough in the upper atmosphere along the Pacific Northwest has kept that dome away from the Bay Area until now. But the weather service said it is expanding and shifting, causing temperatures to rise in the region.
“The dome is expanding westward,” Navarette said. “The trough is a bit more northward and not extending as far down and not as deep as it could be.”
The hot temperatures are expected to persist at least through the weekend, and temperatures may be forecast to be higher as the week progresses, depending on how much influence the heat dome is expected to wield.

title: Tropical Storm Fausto to splash Hawaii , Genevieve sends swells to Mexico
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Rough surf was possible for Hawaii and Mexico on Tuesday thanks to two tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean that forecasters said were sending strong waves to some coastal areas.
Tropical Storm Fausto was expected to pass just north of the Hawaiian islands starting Tuesday night, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Fausto had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was expected to weaken from tropical storm strength early Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Fausto was about 310 miles east-northeast of Honolulu and moving west-northwest near 12 mph. Forecasters said strong currents from the tropical storm could create dangerous conditions on some Hawaii beaches.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Genevieve strengthened to a Category 4, the hurricane center said. Maximum sustained winds were 130 mph for the major hurricane, which was about 590 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.
Swells from Genevieve were reaching Baja California and coastal southwestern Mexico. Forecasters warned of life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
On the forecast track, Genevieve was expected to fluctuate in intensity for about a day before consistently weakening.

title: Californians warned of deadly beach conditions with sneaker waves and rip currents
text:
A beach hazard warning is active across Southern California as officials warn of large waves and life-threatening rip currents along the coast.
The potentially deadly beach conditions are expected along Ventura County beaches, the Malibu coast, Los Angeles County beaches and Orange County.
A National Weather Service advisory is set to remain in effect through Wednesday, July 29, at 5 p.m. The warning also extends farther south to San Diego County and includes the Catalina and Santa Barbara islands.
“Southerly swell is bringing strong, dangerous rip currents & elevated to high surf, especially for Ventura & Los Angeles Co,” the NWS wrote on X. “If you get caught in a rip current, swim parallel to the shoreline to escape, then swim at an angle away from the current, toward shore.”
Beachgoers are advised to take extreme precautions as the southerly swell generates waves between 3 and 6 feet. These conditions create powerful rip currents and a high risk of drowning for even experienced swimmers.
“Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected,” the NWS added. “Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Breaking waves can sweep people off jetties and docks, and into dangerous seas,”
While significant structural damage is unlikely, there is a heightened risk of drowning, the weather service said Tuesday. Strong rip currents may pull swimmers out to sea and large breaking waves can cause injuries, wash individuals off the shore, or capsize small boats near the coastline.
High tides of 6.2 to 7 feet are expected in the evenings through Friday, peaking through Thursday. Combined with Hurricane Genevieve’s swell, minor coastal flooding is most likely on Wednesday and Thursday evenings, the weather service said.
Local authorities recommend staying near lifeguard-protected beaches and avoiding the water entirely during peak surf hours until conditions subside on Wednesday evening.
The advisory comes on the heels of a rescue in Santa Cruz where monstrous waves sucked a young swimmer into massive surf Saturday. As bystanders watched in terror, a 16-year-old lifeguard dove into the water and fought the powerful waves to reach the child and bring him back to shore.
Los Angeles County lifeguards made nearly 2,000 water rescues over the past week, a steep increase from the typical summer weekend average of 200 to 300 rescues, Fox News reported.

title: As an extreme heat warning remains in effect throughout Southern California through at least Sunday night , San Diego - area officials Thursday offered warnings and guidance for those headed outside .
text:
As summer peaks in San Diego County, park officials are shutting down some of San Diego's most grueling and popular recreation areas amid hot temperatures.

title: California teen lifeguard viral rescue captures awe . He was just doing  his duty
text:
He calls it his duty. America calls this 16-year-old California lifeguard a hero
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   
- Video of a 16-year-old lifeguard rescuing a child from pounding waves has gone viral, drawing praise across the country.
- It is the teen’s first summer as a California State Parks lifeguard.
The dramatic footage of a teenage lifeguard saving a child from punishing waves along the California coast has captured the attention of the nation, drawing praise from the shores of Santa Cruz all the way to the White House.
Video of the rescue at Seabright State Beach on Saturday, captured and shared by local photographer Scott Vander Dussen, has gone viral on virtually every social media platform. The footage shows the rookie lifeguard, just 16 years old, holding onto a limp child as massive swells repeatedly pound the duo.
They eventually make it to shore with the help of a second lifeguard. No one suffered any serious injuries, officials said.
President Trump re-shared the video in a post on X — calling the teen a “heroic young man” who he hopes will come to the White House to be properly honored for his valor.
“Very brave, he deserves it!” the president said.
But in a statement, lifeguard Ryder Williams said he was simply doing the job he loves. This summer is his first as a California State Parks lifeguard.
“I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely,” Ryder said in a statement. “This is my job and I love what I do. I’m thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day.”
He described seeing the child “lose his footing in ankle-deep water,” prompting him to run into the waves after him.
“After the first wave, I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard,” he recalled in the statement. “There were two to three more waves before lifeguard Aaron Bohnen entered the water to help me.”
But the teen’s humble retelling underplays a harrowing incident. Vander Dussen, who captured the now-viral video, said the rescue was unlike any he’d seen, given the intensity of the waves and several moments during which he worried the pair might not make it out.
“I’ve seen lots of interventions and rescues,” Vander Dussen said. “I have never seen something like this.”
Shane Williams, Ryder’s father, told the Guardian he was moved watching the video of his son and seeing the world’s reactions.
“I’m super, super proud of him,” Williams told the Guardian.
Lifeguards across the state have made thousands of rescues over the last few days as people have flocked to the coast to escape a long summer heat wave. But in their quest for relief, they’ve found massive, dangerous waves and strong currents fueled by tropical cyclones from the eastern Pacific Ocean, according to the National Weather Service.
Lifeguards with the California State Parks’ Santa Cruz District, which includes Seabright State Beach, performed 34 rescues over the weekend and more than 5,000 “preventative contacts” with beachgoers that may have avoided additional rescues.
Hurricane Genevieve is generating huge waves that will create hazardous beach conditions in Southern California.
Vander Dussen said the waves didn’t initially appear extraordinary at Seabright beach Saturday afternoon, until he heard a crash from what he called a sneaker wave — swells that suddenly surge much farther up a beach and are considered potentially dangerous because they can overtake unsuspecting beachgoers.
As the foaming waters began to retreat, he said he saw a “young man’s head popping up, being carried out to the ocean.” Almost immediately, he said, several people, including himself, alerted the closest lifeguard tower. But they soon realized a lifeguard from a slightly closer tower was already jumping into action: Ryder.
“That’s when I turned the camera on and started to document it,” Vander Dussen said, adding that he “had no idea it was going to be that intense.”
He watched the lifeguard expertly navigate several powerful wave cycles but became worried about the child, who appeared limp during the rescue.
Unsuspecting sneaker waves did and could continue to hit the California coastline during the coastal flood and surf warnings. What to know about sneaker waves.
Eventually, the lifeguard made some progress bringing the boy inland, and with the help of another lifeguard, they made it ashore. The 10-year-old boy who was rescued received some immediate medical attention but was soon released to his parents, Vander Dussen said.
After watching the video several times, Vander Dussen said he became more and more impressed by the young lifeguard.
“Ryder really knows what he’s doing,” he said, calling him a “quintessential Santa Cruz lifeguard.”
Still, he said the teen had remained “incredibly humble,” even as he’s told him about how wide the video has spread.
“It’s a lot to process for a young man,” Vander Dussen said. But he said he deserved the praise, calling him a “local hero” who “knows the ocean in and out.”
“He’s the perfect person you’d want out there rescuing you,” Vander Dussen said.
State officials agreed.
“Our State Park lifeguards courageously risk their own lives every day to keep our visitors safe,” State Parks spokesperson Angelica De La Peña said in a statement. “Their dedication never goes unnoticed and they are truly heroes to their local communities, Californians and the nation.”
Vander Dussen said he initially shared the video not just to raise awareness about water safety, but also to increase support for lifeguards, whom he called key first responders — though federally they aren’t classified as such.
He is hoping the video helps boost support for an effort in Congress to ensure they are considered first responders, which would allow them to be eligible for some specific benefits, especially if something goes wrong on the job.

title: Surf up at U . S . Open in Huntington Beach
text:
Surf’s up at U.S. Open in Huntington Beach
Six-to-eight foot swells greeted competitors at the U.S. Open of Surfing on Wednesday, and that was a welcome sight on the south side of the Huntington Beach Pier.
Huntington Beach resident Bailey Turner was able to hear the welcome sound of cheers from friends and family.
“When I was coming in on my stomach from the pier, I could hear everybody on the pier screaming,” she confirmed.
The 17-year-old advanced in second place in her women’s round of 32 heat with a score of 9.80, just as she had done in the round of 48 of the Challenger Series event on Tuesday. Erin Brooks of Canada won the heat with a two-wave score of 14.00.
Turner, who won the Jack’s Surfboards Pro competition at the same spot in April, will compete against Francisca Veselko of Portugal in the round of 16 as bracket competition begins.
“It’s really good,” Turner said of the pumping conditions, courtesy of Hurricane Genevieve. “I mean, there’s some really good waves, so it’s super-fun. I feel like, the U.S. Open, everybody knows it for being small and pretty grindy. It’s fun to have waves, so everybody gets to show their surfing.”
Sophie McCullough of Australia (15.77), Eden Walla (14.26) and Kirra Pinkerton (14.03) had the highest women’s scores of the day. Walla and Pinkerton are both from San Clemente.
On the men’s side, Keijiro Nishi of Japan was in good spirits after winning his mid-afternoon round of 80 heat with a score of 12.23, outdueling Caleb Tancred of Australia (12.04), who also advanced.
Nishi has a fun personality and spiky red hair to match his red surfboard. As he gave interviews, one of his many supporters waved a large Japanese flag in the background.
“So many Japanese living here,” Nishi said with a smile. “I’m just so happy to make a heat. I just do my best this competition … Good [waves] for me. I like these conditions just fine.”
Jett Schilling of San Clemente narrowly missed advancing. Luke Guinaldo of Huntington Beach, making his U.S. Open debut, was set to open with his round of 80 heat late Wednesday afternoon.
Thursday’s round of 64 will include Huntington Beach’s Kanoa Igarashi, a two-time U.S. Open champion, in the final heat — heat No. 16.
Avalon Gall of Laguna Beach and Tommy Coleman of San Clemente were crowned the event’s longboard champions on Tuesday. It was the second straight U.S. Open longboard title for Gall.

title: Teenage lifeguard rescues child from pounding surf at Santa Cruz beach
text:
President Donald Trump said he wants to invite the teenage lifeguard who rescued a 10-year-old child from the pounding surf at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz Saturday to the White House and honor him.
“We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor,” Trump wrote in a social media post. “Very brave, he deserves it!”
At approximately 3:32 p.m. Saturday on the beach area across from the corner of Mott Avenue and East Cliff Drive, the 16-year-old California State Parks lifeguard was conducting a routine safety check on the shore with another visitor when he spotted a child out in the water. According to State Parks Operations Superintendent Scott Sipes, the child had been knocked down by a crashing wave and was quickly swept out about 15 yards offshore by the powerful current.
Video of the harrowing incident, captured by photographer Scott Vander Dussen and posted to his Instagram account “santacruznow,” begins with the lifeguard clutching the child in waist-high whitewash before a wall of water rushes through the frame as the pair attempts to duck underneath. Sipes said the waves were approximately 8 feet tall and were generated by Hurricane Genevieve, a Category 4 hurricane in the Pacific Ocean near Mexico.
The lifeguard, whose identity is being withheld due to his status as a minor, attempted to pull the child to shore as the water rushed back out to sea, and though he makes some progress, there’s not enough time between wave intervals to reach the dry sand as the cycle of attempting to take cover beneath the heavy shore break continued. Several bystanders entered the water in an attempt to assist with the rescue, but some of them were also inundated by the huge waves and rapid current and were nearly swept out as well, according to the video, which has attracted attention from news outlets across the country.
Eventually, a second lifeguard arrived at the scene and assisted with extracting the child from the water. The child, apparently exhausted and unable to stand, according to the video, was unharmed and was reunited with their mother. Sipes said the teenage lifeguard, healthy and in high spirits after the rescue, clocked back in for another shift Sunday.
Sipes added that the incident Saturday was one of 34 rescues that were performed by local lifeguards in Santa Cruz County over the weekend.
“It’s not always immediately apparent that there is this significant risk because there can be a delay between the intervals of wave sets,” said Sipes. “So conditions could, theoretically, look calm for a moment until another set arrives. And because of the energy and the size of the waves, it can be so detrimental that it would catch an unassuming swimmer by surprise.”
Sipes also said the rescue was a reminder to other members of the public that, unless they are professionally trained, they should remain on the beach and call in for other authorities if they see someone in distress. Otherwise, the bystanders could complicate the effort and require rescuing of their own.
“Sometimes, well-intended people can become overwhelmed themselves and actually add to the rescue,” added Sipes. “We were very fortunate they all made it out.”
Sipes stressed that the dangerous coastal conditions are expected to last at least through Thursday and said members of the public can stay safe by checking in with a lifeguard before entering the water and never turning their back on the ocean.
The National Weather Service has included the county in a beach hazards statement that will last through 5 p.m. Saturday. Breaking waves could reach up to 10 feet tall with sneaker waves and strong rip currents expected to continue to occur as well.

title: Coastal flood advisory for Orange County Coast and San Diego County Coastal Areas from Wednesday to Saturday
text:
Orange County Coast and San Diego County Coastal Areas are under an updated coastal flood advisory which was released by the National Weather Service on Saturday at 2:54 a.m. The advisory is in effect until 3 a.m.
“Minor coastal flooding expected after yesterday evening’s high tide,” according to the NWS San Diego CA. “Swell and surf will subside later today. The high tide and elevated surf will combine to create minor coastal flooding.”
“Flooding of low-lying beach parking lots, boardwalks, and roads. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Breaking waves can sweep people off jetties and docks, and into dangerous seas,” the NWS said. “Inexperienced swimmers should remain out of the water due to dangerous surf conditions.”
Breaking down weather alerts: advisories, watches, and warnings
Flash flood warning: Take action.
A flash flood warning is issued when a flash flood is either imminent or already occurring. In flood-prone areas, it’s crucial to move immediately to higher ground. A flash flood is a sudden and violent inundation that can develop within minutes to hours, and it can even happen in areas not currently experiencing rainfall.
Flood warning: Take action.
A flood warning is declared when flooding is on the verge of happening or is already underway.
Flood advisory: Be aware.
A flood advisory is issued when flooding is not expected to be bad enough to issue a warning. However, it may cause significant inconvenience, and if caution is not exercised, it could lead to situations that may threaten life and/or property.
Flood watch: Be prepared.
A flood watch is issued when conditions are favorable for flooding. It does not mean flooding will occur, but it is possible.
Be flood-ready: Expert guidance from the NWS for your safety
In flood-prone regions or while camping in low-lying areas, understanding and following the NWS flood safety guidelines can be a lifesaver:
Move to higher ground:
If you reside in a flood-prone region or are camping in low-lying terrain, the first step to safety is relocating to higher ground.
Adhere to evacuation orders:
If local authorities issue an evacuation order, heed it promptly. Prior to leaving, secure your home by locking it.
Disconnect utilities and appliances:
If time allows, disconnect your utilities and appliances. This reduces the risk of electrical hazards during flooding.
Avoid basements and submerged areas:
Steer clear of basements or rooms where water has submerged electrical outlets or cords. This helps prevent electrical accidents.
Evacuate promptly for safety:

title: Trump invites teen lifeguard to White House following rescue at California beach
text:
President Donald Trump said he wants to invite the teenage lifeguard who rescued a 10-year-old child from the pounding surf at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz Saturday to the White House and honor him.
“We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor,” Trump wrote in a social media post. “Very brave, he deserves it!”
At approximately 3:32 p.m. Saturday on the beach area across from the corner of Mott Avenue and East Cliff Drive, the 16-year-old California State Parks lifeguard was conducting a routine safety check on the shore with another visitor when he spotted a child out in the water. According to State Parks Operations Superintendent Scott Sipes, the child had been knocked down by a crashing wave and was quickly swept out about 15 yards offshore by the powerful current.
Video of the harrowing incident, captured by photographer Scott Vander Dussen and posted to his Instagram account “santacruznow,” begins with the lifeguard clutching the child in waist-high whitewash before a wall of water rushes through the frame as the pair attempts to duck underneath. Sipes said the waves were approximately 8 feet tall and were generated by Hurricane Genevieve, a Category 4 hurricane in the Pacific Ocean near Mexico.
The lifeguard, whose identity is being withheld due to his status as a minor, attempted to pull the child to shore as the water rushed back out to sea, and though he makes some progress, there’s not enough time between wave intervals to reach the dry sand as the cycle of attempting to take cover beneath the heavy shore break continued. Several bystanders entered the water in an attempt to assist with the rescue, but some of them were also inundated by the huge waves and rapid current and were nearly swept out as well, according to the video, which has attracted attention from news outlets across the country.
Eventually, a second lifeguard arrived at the scene and assisted with extracting the child from the water. The child, apparently exhausted and unable to stand, according to the video, was unharmed and was reunited with their mother. Sipes said the teenage lifeguard, healthy and in high spirits after the rescue, clocked back in for another shift Sunday.
Sipes added that the incident Saturday was one of 34 rescues that were performed by local lifeguards in Santa Cruz County over the weekend.
“It’s not always immediately apparent that there is this significant risk because there can be a delay between the intervals of wave sets,” said Sipes. “So conditions could, theoretically, look calm for a moment until another set arrives. And because of the energy and the size of the waves, it can be so detrimental that it would catch an unassuming swimmer by surprise.”
Sipes also said the rescue was a reminder to other members of the public that, unless they are professionally trained, they should remain on the beach and call in for other authorities if they see someone in distress. Otherwise, the bystanders could complicate the effort and require rescuing of their own.
“Sometimes, well-intended people can become overwhelmed themselves and actually add to the rescue,” added Sipes. “We were very fortunate they all made it out.”
Sipes stressed that the dangerous coastal conditions are expected to last at least through Thursday and said members of the public can stay safe by checking in with a lifeguard before entering the water and never turning their back on the ocean.
The National Weather Service has included the county in a beach hazards statement that will last through 5 p.m. Saturday. Breaking waves could reach up to 10 feet tall with sneaker waves and strong rip currents expected to continue to occur as well.

Hazardous beach conditions remain the biggest weather concern across the Central Coast this week. A long-period south swell continues to produce large breaking waves, dangerous rip currents, and an increased risk of sneaker waves through at least midweek. More than two dozen water rescues were reported along the California coast Sunday, serving as a reminder to never turn your back on the ocean. If you're heading to the beach, stay well back from the water's edge, avoid rocks and jetties, and keep a close eye on one another.
Away from the coast, temperatures will remain near normal today before a gradual warming trend begins midweek. Inland valleys and mountain communities will see temperatures climb each day, with moderate heat expected by next weekend.
The warming temperatures combined with breezy afternoon onshore winds and increasingly dry vegetation will elevate wildfire concerns this week. The greatest risk will be across the higher terrain of the Santa Lucia Mountains, where any new fire could spread quickly. Avoid activities that could create sparks, especially during the warmest and windiest parts of the day. If you are going to have a campfire, be sure it's contained in a designated area and you have a shovel, bucket of water, and your campfire permit.
Fires, campfires, and stoves are currently prohibited in Los Padres National Forest, where only gas-powered stoves may be used by individuals with their valid CA Campfire Permit.
Looking ahead, category 5 hurricane Genevieve may influence the weather pattern later this week, but for now it is expected to harmlessly spin to the northwest with no direct impacts expected to the Central Coast.

title: Why New England is in for days of soaking rain
text:
Hi, I’m Dave Epstein, a meteorologist for the Globe, guest-writing today’s Starting Point, and I’ve been tracking the latest on our next round of soaking rain that’s about to overtake New England this week.
But first, here’s what else is going on:
- Democrats are planning to blow up the primary schedule, which includes downgrading New Hampshire from being the first battleground. Here’s what the new game plan means.
- President Trump’s administration is trying to leverage the Supreme Court’s power to limit mail-in ballots. This comes ahead of a crucial battle as both parties attempt to gain control of the House and Senate this November.
- Wildfires across Spain and France are causing record destruction. Hundreds of thousands of residents have been forced to evacuate.
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.
TODAY’S STARTING POINT
We’ve enjoyed plenty of sunshine and beautiful conditions to start the week, but beginning today, we’ll see our weather pattern in New England gradually shift — meaning storm activity, with rainfall, scattered thunderstorms, and periods of significant heavy downpours that could potentially lead to localized flash flooding.
Over 2 inches of rain is possible from late Tuesday through Thursday in parts of Southern New England.
What’s driving all of this unsettled weather?
An upper-level trough, or dip in the jet stream, will be rotating down over New England from the middle to the end of the week. The energy released along this wave in the atmosphere will kick off a low-pressure system at the surface, a rather unusual low for two reasons: its storm track for this time of year and its strength.
Just like during winter when the exact track of a storm determines where the heaviest snow falls, so too will the exact track of this storm ultimately translate into where the heaviest rain ends up.
Several of the models keep the highest risk for urban street flooding or even potential flash flooding over Central and Western Massachusetts and Connecticut.
The breakdown
A few areas in Western Massachusetts will see showers starting Tuesday afternoon, but for the most part, eastern areas will stay dry through most of the day. Because we’re going to see dew points rise significantly later Tuesday into Wednesday, that available moisture will be high and could produce heavy downpours.
When Greater Boston is expected to see the rain is a bit sketchy.
Areas over Southeastern Massachusetts might not see any rainfall until Wednesday, while areas north and west of I-495 could see some showers as early as Tuesday evening.

title: A record - challenging heat dome is about to bake the West with the summer hottest temperatures so far
text:
An unusually strong heat dome will scorch much of the western United States this weekend, bringing the hottest temperatures so far this year to tens of millions from California to Canada.
Dozens of record highs are expected to fall in at least 12 states in the West through the weekend with nearly 50 million people under heat alerts.
High temperatures will climb between 10 to nearly 20 degrees hotter than they should be — even for the peak of summer — from Southern California to the northern Rockies and Plains from Friday through Tuesday. Death Valley, California, is forecast to see the hottest temperature of this heat wave: a blistering 126 degrees.
This is the latest in a spate of record-breaking heat waves that have affected the US and Europe simultaneously this summer. Human-caused climate change is making heat waves like this one more likely to occur, as well as more intense and longer-lasting, studies show. Particularly strong and slow-moving heat domes are also possibly becoming more common as the world warms, though this is an area of active research.
The heat dome responsible for this heat wave may also set records for its intensity in parts of Southern California and Arizona. Heat domes act like a lid on a pot, trapping and enhancing hot air beneath them. This one is expected to reach even higher in the atmosphere than typical, and that means it can trap even more air below it, raising the ceiling on just how extreme surface temperatures can get.
Nearly 12 million people across the Southwest, Mountain West and northern Great Plains are under a Level 4 of 4 "extreme" heat risk Saturday and Sunday, with an additional 20 million people under a Level 3 of 4 "major" heat risk. Heat at this level will affect anyone without access to cooling and hydration, the National Weather Service warns.
The weekend heat may just be the first wave of extreme temperatures from this heat dome as it settles in for the long haul, with more hot weather predicted in large parts of the West beginning on August 6.
Dangerous, record-setting heat
By August 4, around 10% of the continental US will record the hottest day of the year so far.
Billings, Montana, is forecast to hit 106 degrees on Saturday, breaking its August record. The city recorded its hottest-ever temperature of 111 degrees just two weeks ago. Salt Lake City will approach its August record with a forecast of 104 on Saturday, on the heels of breaking its all-time record high earlier this month.
In California, where highs across much of the state's interior will reach 100 to 110 degrees, anyone seeking relief at the beaches will need to be cautious: Far offshore Hurricane Genevieve will send large waves and rip currents along the southern portion of the state. Lifeguards with the Los Angeles County Fire Department performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues last week as millions visited area beaches, the department said in a post on social media.
Phoenix and Tucson, Arizona, and Las Vegas are all expected to rise well above 110 degrees. In Maricopa County, home to Phoenix, there have been 40 confirmed heat-related deaths so far this year, county data shows, with months of summer heat still to come.
Heat is the deadliest type of extreme weather in the US, with a higher annual average death toll than tornadoes, hurricanes and lightning combined, National Weather Service statistics show. Emergency room visits for heat-related illness surge on "major" and "extreme" risk days, according to the weather service.
Overnight lows will also remain nearly 10 degrees above normal across the West, offering little relief even after dark. This lack of a cooldown is especially dangerous as it gives the body less time to recover before the next day's heat builds again.
Heat triggers a wave of worrying impacts
The heat wave is also worsening wildfire and water concerns across the West, particularly the parched Colorado River Basin.
Much of the river basin as well as higher elevations in central and Southern California saw below average snowfall this past winter. This heat will dry out the ground further, making the region more vulnerable to wildfires.
Other concerns center on water and energy supplies, given the beleaguered state of the river basin.
The combined water level of Lake Mead and Lake Powell, two of the biggest US reservoirs, is at a historic low and continues to drop.
These reservoirs, together with the river basin overall, provide water to tens of millions of people. The heat wave will only exacerbate the rate of evaporation and decline in water levels from these critical resources.

title: SoCal has had  so many heat waves , but this next one is a doozy
text:
SoCal has had ‘so many heat waves,’ but this next one is a doozy: What to know
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   
- Southern California faces an extreme heat wave beginning Friday.
- Forecasters warn of heightened risks of heat illness and large wildfires.
Extreme heat is set to roll into Southern California, extending a summer of misery-making stickiness and hot temperatures.
“We’ve had so many heat waves,” said V. Kelly Turner, who leads the heat research group at the UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation. “There’s a slight reprieve between them, but not really.”
The weekend is expected to bring dangerous heat starting Friday, with forecasters warning of elevated risks of heat illness and large wildfires.
High pressure over Arizona will expand west through the weekend, reaching California’s interior deserts and potentially as far west as the coast, according to the National Weather Service. That will send temperatures about 10 degrees above normal in many areas, possibly setting new daily records, a weather service forecast stated.
“The main message is: Regardless of whether we are meeting or exceeding records, this is an extreme heat event that will take place,” said Ariel Cohen, meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service in Oxnard. The weather service has issued an extreme heat warning for much of the area, outside of the coast, from Friday through Sunday.
Forecasters are calling for highs of 95 to 110 degrees in the valleys, with portions of the Antelope Valley potentially reaching 115 degrees, and 100 to 110 across the Inland Empire and high desert, with the low desert potentially nearing 120 degrees.
Overnight temperatures won’t fall much below 70 degrees in many locations near Los Angeles, increasing the risk of heat stress, Cohen said.
Humidity levels dipped through Wednesday, allowing for more overnight cooling and providing a bit of relief, forecasters said. But models suggest that moisture could return later in the week and into the weekend, according to the weather service.
The majority of Southern California, except for the immediate coastline, will see an enhanced risk of large wildfires Friday through Sunday, when conditions will be hottest and driest, said Kristen Stewart, meteorologist with the U.S. Forest Service. Areas of particular concern include the foothills of the San Joaquin Valley and the region’s lower mountain areas, she said.
“Our fuels have been drying out over time and are at pretty much critical levels right now,” she said.
In Calabasas, residents are outraged by scheduled overnight power outages in the coming days, while Southern California Edison crews make infrastructure upgrades in an effort to lower wildfire risks. Several hundred customers will be affected at various times.
“On a heat wave. It’s horrible, it’s unbearable,” resident Jonathan Bobbitt told CBS News.
The utility company said they had notified all customers two weeks ago. The scheduled outages were pushed to slightly later in the night, during cooler hours, but the company said it could not cancel the planned upgrades altogether.
Southern California Edison spokesperson David Eisenhauer said the scheduled outages were “chosen in coordination with the city to avoid hottest hours of the day and minimize impacts to the community,” although the company understands “any outage can be a hardship.”
Forecasters are calling for a slow cooling trend starting Sunday but warned that temperatures would still be above normal and would remain that way for the foreseeable future as the high pressure persists.
Southern California has seen a hot and unusually muggy summer, in part due to warm ocean temperatures.
Such long-lasting events worsen the stress heat puts on people’s bodies, and so does humidity, which can also render some solutions, such as taking cover in the shade, less effective, Turner said.
Climate change from the burning of fossil fuels has resulted in hotter, more frequent heat waves, said David Eisenman, professor of medicine and co-director of the UCLA Center for Healthy Climate Solutions.
“Also, importantly, the nighttime doesn’t cool down like it used to, so our bodies are not able to recover in the same way,” he said.
In addition to causing death and illness directly, extreme heat can exacerbate heart, lung and kidney disease, as well as mental health problems, he said.
People can lessen the stress by staying inside somewhere that has air conditioning, taking the shadiest route possible when spending time outside, and submerging themselves in water — even if it’s just a cold foot bath, Turner said. She calls the recommendations the “big three.”
“Those are the ones that can reliably make your body work less hard to cool itself down,” she said.
Cohen, of the weather service, said that people should also stay hydrated and refrain from leaving children or pets in vehicles. Those who must be outside are encouraged to wear lightweight, loose-fitting clothing and limit strenuous activities to the early morning or evening, he said.
Forecasters warned that those seeking to escape the heat with a trip to the beach should take care, as a large south swell from Hurricane Genevieve will continue to result in big waves. Southern California lifeguards reported performing thousands of rescues last weekend amid crowded conditions, rough surf and strong rip currents.
A high surf advisory is in effect through Saturday evening, with forecasters warning the risks are especially acute for south-facing beaches, including Manhattan Beach to Port Hueneme along the Malibu coast, and from Long Beach to the Palos Verdes Peninsula.
The weather service also issued a coastal flood advisory for the Ventura and L.A. County coasts from Wednesday evening through Friday due to the swell.
Times staff writer Suhauna Hussain contributed to this report.

title: August is around the corner . Pile on the heat
text:
One of the hottest weekends of the year (so far) is on tap for Southern California
It looks like the first weekend of August is going to look a lot like most of the month of July: hot and humid.
But the coming heat wave may be especially intense.
Most of Southern California has faced repeated heat advisories over the last few weeks. Ahead of this weekend, though, the National Weather Service has issued more severe extreme heat warnings for almost the entire region. Those will be in effect from 10 a.m. Friday through Sunday evening.
Temperatures are expected to peak on Saturday, when forecasters say highs could get within one or two degrees of daily records.
Parts of the San Fernando Valley, San Gabriel Valley and Inland Empire will see highs well over 100 degrees. Intermediate areas between the coasts and the valleys, including downtown Los Angeles, will be mostly in the upper 80s to mid-90s. Coasts will be mostly in the 80s.
Humidity continues to add to the discomfort and make it harder to cool down at night.
Forecasters say the highest humidity will be along the coast, as high ocean temperatures drive up the moisture in the air. Those areas could see some dense fog on Friday morning.
The combination of heat and humidity will pose a particularly high risk for people over 65, young children, people who work — or spend a lot of time — outside and those without access to air conditioning.
Officials are warning against leaving children and pets in unattended vehicles. Under such extreme heat, temperatures inside a car can reach lethal levels in a matter of minutes.
Making sense of heat forecasts
Southern Californians are no strangers to hot weather in the summer, but heat waves are getting hotter, longer and more frequent as the climate changes.
So you should know the words forecasters use to describe these weather events — and the risks they pose.
- Heat advisory: Advisories are issued when temperatures are expected to be hot enough to cause discomfort and potentially lead to heat-related illnesses, especially for more vulnerable populations like young children and the elderly.
- Extreme heat watch: Watches are essentially forecasts for upcoming periods of extreme heat. Forecasters say heat watches often cover wide areas and will be revised into more focused warnings and advisories as conditions become clearer over time. Watches are a good time to prepare for extreme heat.
- Extreme heat warning: Warnings are issued when heat levels are or will likely become extremely dangerous. Under extreme heat warnings, it's a good idea to avoid strenuous outdoor activity, stay hydrated and help loved ones and pets stay cool.
Protect free press
Fire weather
Despite the humidity, this weekend’s heat wave is also going to drive up the risk of wildfires.
Inland areas, where the humidity is lower than on the coast, will be most prone to fires. The high temperatures, combined with possible wind, mean any fires that start could have the potential to grow large.
Wind gusts could get up to 45 mph in places, with the strongest expected along the 5 Freeway corridor near the Grapevine and in southwestern Santa Barbara County.
About 90% of California wildfires are sparked by people.
Beachgoers beware
A National Weather Service high surf advisory is in place through Saturday afternoon for all Southern California beaches — from San Diego County through Santa Barbara County, including Catalina and Santa Barbara islands.
Large, breaking waves and strong rip currents are the biggest risk to beachgoers, with the most dangerous conditions on south-facing beaches. Rip currents can pull swimmers and surfers out to sea. Large waves can cause injury, wash people off rocks and capsize small boats.
Forecasters recommend staying out of the water, if possible. If you do go swimming, stay near lifeguards, heed their advice and stay off of tidal rocks and jetties.
Beach safety tips
Officials recommend checking surf conditions before heading to the beach.
If you do go in the water, stay near staffed lifeguard stations and listen to lifeguards' instructions. They're there for your safety.
It’s also a good idea to stay off of tidal rocks and jetties. Big waves can sneak up on you.
If you end up caught in a rip current while swimming, don't panic. Stay calm and float as much as possible to conserve energy. To escape the current, swim parallel to the beach, then at an angle toward the beach. Do not try to swim against the current. If you can’t reach the shore, call and wave for help.
The heatwave is also adding to the risk as it will likely drive more people to the beach, potentially putting them in harm's way.
Forecasters also issued a coastal flooding advisory that will be in effect through much of Saturday for the SoCal coastline and Channel Islands.
Flooding is likely around high tide. It could affect low-lying areas of beaches, walkways and parking lots, but significant damage to roads or structures is not expected.
The highest tides will likely be tonight, coinciding with the peak of a storm swell from Hurricane Genevieve, which has been whirling hundreds of miles off the coast of Mexico since it formed last week.
Genevieve, along with swells from other Pacific storms, are also responsible for the waves and rip currents.

text:

covers important issues that affect the everyday lives of Southern Californians.
