Topline:
If you missed out on those coveted tickets for Olivia Rodrigo’s music festival in Irvine, you’re in luck. There’s a giveaway happening, but you have to join a volunteer drive to get a chance.
How it works: The nonprofit L.A. Works is calling the giveaway Daisy Chain Reaction. To get a chance at one of the 125 pairs of tickets, you have to volunteer at one of their approved events.
The caveat: The volunteer drive has a collective hours requirement. That means volunteers need to work together to rack up at least 1,000 hours by Aug. 20, which “unlocks” the giveaway portion. The winners will be chosen at random.
Read on…. to learn more about how it works and where you can go.
Olivia Rodrigo’s upcoming Daisy Chain Fields festival in Irvine sold out brutally fast. If you missed out on tickets, you’re in luck.
The “Driver’s License” artist has partnered with the nonprofit L.A. Works to give Livies a chance at experiencing the all-woman lineup on Aug. 29. The organization is giving out 125 pairs of tickets — with a catch.
How the giveaway works
L.A. Works is determining who gets the general admission tickets through a “volunteer drive” called Daisy Chain Reaction. The drive’s events are focused on supporting women and girls in Southern California.
For a chance to win, your first step is to sign up to volunteer with L.A. Works. Then, the drive has to hit a collective hours goal for the giveaway to be “unlocked.” Between now and 7 p.m. Aug. 20, volunteers need to log at least 1,000 verified hours.
Each participant gets entered into the giveaway based on how many verified hours they volunteered. One hour counts as one entry (no maximum), so the more you volunteer, the higher your chances.
The winners will be picked through a random drawing, and you’ll be contacted via email if you get a pair. To be eligible you must:
Be at least 18 years old at the time of winning
Have an active L.A. Works account in good standing
Opt in to the giveaway when registering for an eligible Daisy Chain Reaction volunteer opportunity
Be a resident of the U.S.
Where to volunteer
The volunteer opportunities are based in Los Angeles and Orange counties. Some may have a waitlist.
Currently, there are 16 events (many of them recurring) spread out across L.A. County. That includes serving breakfast near MacArthur Park, helping with soil restoration in Altadena and passing out back-to-school backpacks in Montebello.
On the other hand, Orange County currently has just three on the roster. That includes packing food in Irvine and helping out at a STEM event for middle-school girls in Santa Ana. L.A. Works says it’s trying to add more O.C. events.
You can find all of the volunteer opportunities here — just make sure the one you pick has “DCR” in the title or mentions the giveaway in the description.
If you sign up, make sure you can attend. Participants who no-show more than one day will be disqualified from the giveaway.

What we know: A city official who spoke to LAist on the condition they not be named because they weren't authorized to speak on the record confirmed that the safety design approved by the mayor includes widening portions of the road.
Why it matters: The plan comes after years of controversy over how to make the one-mile stretch of the road near Griffith Park safer. Bass halted a plan to reduce lanes on the road earlier this year.
Read on ... for more about how the city is approaching safety on the busy road.
In a statement Friday to LAist, the mayor’s office said L.A. Mayor Karen Bass’ plan for the busy road near Griffith Park will “improve traffic, cycling and pedestrian safety, and keep traffic flowing."
The office said the plan includes adding a protected left-turn lane and protected bike lanes to the 1-mile stretch of Forest Lawn Drive and maintains the roadway's four existing lanes.
The mayor’s office did not respond to additional questions from LAist, including whether Bass’ plan will reduce speeding on the road, whether there’s a timeline for implementation and how soon the community will be informed about specifics.
A city official who spoke to LAist on condition they not be named because they weren't authorized to speak on the record confirmed that the safety design approved by the mayor includes widening portions of the road. Road widening was first proposed by a consultant for Forest Lawn Memorial Parks and Mortuaries.
Forest Lawn Memorial Parks operates a chain of cemeteries, including one in the Hollywood Hills that can only be accessed along Forest Lawn Drive. The company was a longtime opponent of a prior proposal to reduce lanes on the roadway that Bass halted in May.
Forest Lawn Memorial Parks worked to block that plan due to concerns that it would increase traffic congestion and impede access to its Hollywood Hills cemetery.
The exact price tag for Bass’ latest plan announced Friday is unclear.
City transportation department records obtained by LAist show a proposal to widen the road developed by a consultant for Forest Lawn Memorial Parks would cost nearly five times more than the plan to reduce lanes on Forest Lawn Drive.
City transportation staff said in an analysis that the consultant’s road widening plan would have “low” potential to slow speeding cars, according to the public records.
The L.A. Department of Transportation said in a statement that it is “coordinating with the Bureau of Engineering on advancing the Mayor's direction.”
Details of the original plan Bass halted in May
The proposal that almost went ahead before Bass halted it would have cut the number of lanes from four to three, transforming the road into two through-lanes and one center turn lane. The bumpy, cracked, pothole-ridden road would also have been resurfaced.
The goal was to slow cars and address the nearly 100 traffic collisions, including four deadly ones, the road has seen since 2013.
Brian Taylor, a research professor of urban planning and public policy at UCLA, told LAist that research on how so-called road diets improve safety is “unequivocal,” adding that there is a significant reduction in crashes and injuries when lanes are reduced.
The plan to reduce lanes came with a $618,000 price tag that would have covered the costs of repainting new lanes on the road and installing plastic posts to fortify the bike lanes. Those costs would have been covered through the city’s existing resources for road improvements,according to the city’s transportation department.
The road has become an issue in L.A.’s tight mayoral race
The future of Forest Lawn Drive has become a touchpoint in the L.A. mayor’s race, where Bass is facing L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, whose district includes this portion of Forest Lawn Drive and whose office initiated the project in 2022.
At an August campaign event about Forest Lawn Drive, following a fatal collision on the road, Raman said one reason she’s running for mayor is so “lifesaving street safety improvements are not stymied and are not politicized.”
The road is the sole point of entry to two major cemeteries, the Hollywood Hills locations of Forest Lawn Memorial Parks and Mount Sinai Memorial Parks.
The cemeteries, neighborhood groups and state legislators opposed the lane reduction plan, citing concerns about traffic congestion, especially during funeral processions, and ease of access.
In a joint statement to LAist in August, the cemeteries praised Bass’ decision to find a new approach for the road, saying it “demonstrated responsive leadership and a willingness to get this right.” The cemeteries did not respond to LAist’s requests for a follow-up.
After the mayor paused the lane-reduction plan, the city delayed resurfacing Forest Lawn Drive.

The state’s involvement
State legislators representing L.A. had pressed the mayor in a letter in April about the project, saying traffic lane reductions would be “disastrous to the operation of key cemeteries” in the area and calling for more review of alternatives.
In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill that makes it more difficult to reduce lanes on Forest Lawn Drive.

The investigation by the office of inspector general for the high-speed rail project found that some consultants flew first class, hailed luxury rides and traveled to a night club, a cigar lounge and numerous restaurants, bars and residences, sometimes after hours, on taxpayers’ dime.

In some cases, agency staff didn’t even know about the trips until they received invoices.

Board chair Steve Kawa told reporters afterward that the decision “adds additional eyes and ears and authority” over issues exposed by the investigation.
“We are not just gonna sit back and ignore that we had this travel issue,” he said. “Not one dollar of California taxpayer dollars should be misused.”
“I am outraged that we would be treated like a piggy bank for these kinds of expenditures.”
Several board members slammed the consultants for the travel expenses. Lynn Schenk, who has served on the board since 2003, said the spending suggests a troubling pattern and deserves a deeper dive.
“I am outraged that we would be treated like a piggy bank for these kinds of expenditures,” she said during the board meeting. “And it says to me that there are other expenditures that are being treated this way.”
Board member Henry Perea suggested the travel payments are so egregious that the state should end its contract with the firms right away, something Gov. Gavin Newsom has also floated. However, Perea said he worried that doing so could set back the long-delayed rail project even further.
“I’d terminate these four [contracts] tomorrow or today, but I understand there’s a question of operational needs that we have with these folks,” he said.
But the board did not grill the authority’s top executives for failing to catch the behavior, even though the probe revealed that consultants told agency staff many times that they were traveling at the request of the agency’s top officers, including Choudri.
In response to the investigation, the authority paused all travel payments to the four consulting firms in question and has started reviewing their claims and training staff, executives and consultants on travel policies, said the authority’s Chief Financial Officer Jamey Matalka.
One legal consultant was paid $40,800 in travel reimbursements and an additional $86,500 in “travel time” for 30 trips between Denver and Sacramento in a year. When questioned about whether he needed to attend the meetings in person, he said Choudri had requested his presence so he did not need to justify it and that it would not be appropriate for him to question Choudri’s direction, “as other consultants in other Authority offices are learning the hard way.”
In response to the investigation, the authority paused all travel payments to the four consulting firms in question and has started reviewing their claims and training staff, executives and consultants on travel policies, said the authority’s Chief Financial Officer Jamey Matalka. The firms are: KPMG LLP, a global financial consulting firm; Nossaman LLP, a national law firm; AECOM-Fluor Joint Venture, which manages and coordinates the authority’s projects, and SYSTRA/TYPSA Joint Venture, which provides tracks and systems design.
The agency is seeking to recoup all questionable travel payments, he said Friday.
“We remain committed [and] we take full responsibility and accountability to fix if there was something broken in the system,” Choudri told the board.
Choudri also told board members that the agency has taken “disciplinary actions” against some consultants but did not clarify what they were. Choudri did not speak to reporters following the meeting.
Assembly Minority Leader Alexandra Macedo, a Visilia Republican, called for Choudri’s firing in a Thursday letter to the board. She accused him of demonstrating a “pattern of misuse of taxpayer dollars and abuse of public trust.”
“At a time when California families face unbearable financial pressures to cover essential household needs including rent, utilities and transportation, the routine approval of improper consultant expenses represents a severe breach of fiduciary responsibility,” she wrote.
‘They should all be here’
Of the four consulting firms investigated, only one sent representatives Friday.
Veronica Siranosian, an executive at AECOM-Fluor Joint Venture, told the board the company reviewed its travel invoices and found “no substantive departures from the established public processes.”
The inspector general’s investigation found nearly $380,000 in travel expenses by the company’s consultants that were not allowed under state regulations or the company’s contract with the state.
Nevertheless, another AECOM executive, Mike Burns, said the company has identified only about $1,000 in expenses it overbilled the state, including for an Uber ride, parking in a garage that charged a higher rate than surrounding buildings and a flight that was on an international carrier instead of an American airline.
In some cases, Burns stressed, the dollar difference was small. He said the company’s consultants once took an $86 Uber ride in an electric vehicle whereas the standard policy would require an $84 Uber X instead. “It was a $2 differentiation,” he said. “There’s some nominal incidences like that.”
Schenk gasped.
“Surely you are not saying that we are sitting here for these hours going through this … for a $2 difference,” she said. “And surely you will at least acknowledge that these instances show a disregard at the very least for state and high-speed rail requirements.”
“It’s gonna take a lot of $2 differences in Uber rides to get to the $380,000 that you guys billed the state of California,” said Vice Chair Anthony Williams.
Board member Emily Cohen slammed the consulting firms that did not appear Friday.
“They should all be here. Unbelievable.”
Authority to step up training, improve policy
Matalka said the authority would implement all the fixes the inspector general’s office recommended. He said the authority would, by the end of the year, create a new travel approval form requiring more details.
By the end of March, he said, it would establish a “consistent, uniform process” for advance travel approvals, ramp up training, create a list of approved office locations for consultants, recoup misspent state funding and use AI to flag travel requests that potentially violate policies.
But much of the steps seems like “basic oversight,” Schenk said. “Why weren’t we doing this at the outset?” she asked. “What is the root cause?”
Matalka said some questionable travel requests slipped through the cracks because staff did not review them deep enough.
“Training needs to be done so that we make sure you are not just looking at the labor hours, you are not just looking at the lodging rate,” he said. “You need to actually Google the address, look at the timestamp, look at some of the very small print on the fare class.”
The authority frequently approved expenses with vague justifications, such as “typical M-F week” trips, and approved travel at the request of executives without asking why. One consultant flew to California from Denver 20 times during the two-year period to “meet with the executive team” or attend executive meetings, without explaining why the meetings couldn’t have been remote, the investigation says.
The high-speed rail project is already long delayed and over its projected budget: In 2008, voters approved a $10 billion bond to build a high-speed rail line from San Francisco to Los Angeles by 2020 for an estimated $45 billion. The project is now estimated to cost between $126 billion and $231 billion, with a full buildout expected by 2040, according to the authority’s latest business plan. Current plans call for building a first leg linking Merced to Bakersfield.

Topline:
With state resources having been cut, a former state biologist launches her own bear coexistence business.
Why it matters: It’s the time of year when black bears are beefing up — often on trash — in Southern California’s foothill communities. In recent years, these areas have seen a rise in conflicts with bears.
Read on ... for more on why one biologist who lost her job with the state is starting her own business to help communities live with bears.
It’s that time of year when black bears are beefing up, often on trash, in Southern California’s foothill communities.
From fall to early winter, bears quadruple their food intake in preparation for the cooler months — bears here don’t really hibernate given our mild weather and plethora of resources, but they do slow down during the winter (as we all should). And right now, mother bears are looking to find a safe place to den and have their cubs.
Bears aren’t just roaming the roads of mountain towns either. They’re in suburban neighborhood streets along the 210 Freeway corridor — including Altadena, Sierra Madre and Monrovia — and even in Encino and Tarzana.
This time of year is when humans and bears might come into conflict more frequently, says a former biologist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
“You're going to see those bears just eating ravenously, foraging all day for food, and then also they're going to start looking for these potential denning sites under our crawl spaces, unfortunately,” said Jessica West, a human-wildlife conflict specialist who over the last five years worked for the state on bear coexistence efforts from Santa Barbara to San Diego.
Nearly 60,000 black bears are estimated to live in California. Here in Southern California, the estimate is around 2,000, according to the latest count by the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife.
Who's that bear?
Though they may appear brown or blond, black bears are the only species of bear in California.
For thousands of years, brown bears, also called grizzly bears, were the main bear of the California landscape, including here in Southern California. But European and American settlers killed them all off by the early 1900s.
Evidence of black bears in Southern California dates to about 25,000 years ago. The theory is they headed farther north in the middle of the Ice Age as the landscape here got a lot drier and the ancient forest disappeared.
So how did black bears come back? They were brought here by the government from Yosemite as a tourist attraction. (Wild right? If you want to dig deeper, listen to our podcast about black bears in Southern California.)
Black bears are omnivores and opportunists. They primarily eat plants and bugs, but they’ll also eat animal carcasses, small mammals and, of course, whatever’s in your trash.
State resources to help communities coexist with bears have been cut. That includes West, who was the sole wildlife conflict biologist serving Southern California counties. Gov. Gavin Newsom just signed a bill into law that aims to bring some of those resources back, but in the meantime, the need remains.
“More than ever, people and bears are sharing space,” West said. "The fact is that they're here and they're not going anywhere, and we're here as humans and we're not going anywhere.”
Neither did West’s passion for wildlife coexistence when she was laid off. That’s why she just launched her own business to help fill the resource gap: Wild Neighbor.
Jessica West, a bear biologist, installs an "unwelcome" mat at a home. The electrified mat helps keeps curious bears away.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
An "unwelcome" mat with bear prints outside of a home in Ojai.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
She offers detailed property assessments and recommendations for $150. She focuses primarily on prevention, such as strategically placing electric wiring and “unwelcome” mats to secure crawl spaces, trash and other vulnerable areas, which can cost $350 to around $900 depending on the home. She also rents such equipment if residents prefer. West works with manufacturers of electric bear-resistant tools that have been vetted for fire safety and bear conflict.
“What the science shows is that the most effective deterrent that we have at this point in time in our tool belt for bears is electricity,” West said. “There's really nothing like that in the wild for bears. It's a very novel stimulus for them.”
Don't attract bears
Get a bear-resistant trash can if your city offers it and it fits your budget. If you can’t, take your trash out as close to trash pickup as possible. (GPS collar data has shown that bears actually learn trash day schedules.) Or keep your trash inside a secure structure, like a closed garage.
Get rid of bird seed and hummingbird nectar feeders.
Bears have extremely powerful noses and can squeeze through even small opened windows to get to a refrigerator. So if bears are present in your neighborhood, keep accessible windows closed and locked as much as possible.
If a bear has already gotten into your crawl space, West can be hired to coax it out. But if a mother bear with cubs is under the house, West won’t evict them. Instead, she’ll work with the property owner to monitor the situation until the bear family leaves.
“We really want to avoid potentially orphaning those cubs,” she said.
It’s best to avoid allowing a bear to get into your crawl space or trash in the first place, West said. When bears become too accustomed to humans and eating human food, the risk of injury to people and pets rises. And the bears themselves are more likely to be euthanized.
In 2023, California hit a tragic milestone: It was the state’s first documented killing of a human by a black bear, in Northern California. In Southern California, foothill communities such as Sierra Madre have seen several bear-related injuries in recent years (more on that in our 2024 podcast on this topic). Several bears, including a well-known one in La Cañada Flintridge, have also been euthanized in recent years.
In the vast majority of cases, this is preventable, West said, if residents take a little responsibility for securing their own properties. That can also save thousands of dollars in damage caused by a bear.
Since West is no longer with the state, she can’t trap bears that have risen to the point of becoming a problem — for example, those that learn how to regularly get into homes or cars, or have lost their fear of humans. She does encourage her clients to share sightings and any concerning conflicts with the Department of Fish and Wildlife, but she doesn’t share anything herself without clients’ permission. (Learn how to report bear sightings or human-bear conflict here.)
West said that in lieu of state resources, companies like hers may become more common.
“What [clients] can expect is someone who is going to listen to them, and someone who is passionate about their job and really wants to help them,” West said. “Because at the end of the day, I'm a bear biologist by training. I love bears, but my whole goal in all of this is to help people. Because if we help people, we're also helping bears.”

Orange County cities are close to finalizing ballot measures that will go before voters in the November general election.
Why it matters: Local governments have until Aug. 7 to call a local measure election for the November ballot. Registrar of Voters Bob Page told LAist that the county encourages cities to file much earlier to allow time for public review, arguments and analysis, as well as document processing.

Orange County cities are close to finalizing what ballot measures will go before voters in the November general election.
It’s never too early to be prepared, so here’s what we know is coming so far.
Santa Ana: Could a sales tax rate be permanent?
Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax increase — called Measure X — is supposed to decrease in 2029 and then completely go away by 2039. Public officials have said the loss of Measure X could mean the city loses millions of dollars in revenue.
The tax measure was approved by voters in 2018. Money from the tax has helped the city fund street maintenance, public safety, youth services and homelessness services.
Currently, large businesses have a $200 limit for taxes to operate in the city. For example, big box stores like Home Depot and Target in Costa Mesa only pay $200 a year in business license taxes. The change, if approved, could increase that to as high as $15,000 based on gross income.
Small businesses — which the city defines as those with $500,000 or less in gross income — will not be affected.
Irvine: Ranked-choice voting
In Irvine, voters will be asked whether the city should switch the local election system to ranked-choice voting in 2028.
The system would allow voters to rank their candidates in order of preference instead of casting a vote for one candidate.
If approved, the change would only take effect if the costs stay below 0.23% of the city’s general fund. If the switch goes above that amount, the ranked-choice voting system could be delayed until a future election.
Orange: Is a city charter coming?
Orange is currently a general law city bound by state law and mandates. Voters will decide if Orange should become a charter city, joining other municipal governments like Los Angeles, Santa Ana and Huntington Beach.
Charter cities still have to follow state and federal laws, but can establish their own rules on issues such as mayoral authority, term limits and financial management.
Some council members say the move will give the city more local control over planning, contracting and revenue. Opponents worry that the council is moving too fast on the charter measure instead of tackling the city’s financial crisis head-on.

Topline:
With state resources having been cut, a former state biologist launches her own bear coexistence business.
Why it matters: It’s the time of year when black bears are beefing up — often on trash — in Southern California’s foothill communities. In recent years, these areas have seen a rise in conflicts with bears.
Read on ... for more on why one biologist who lost her job with the state is starting her own business to help communities live with bears.
It’s that time of year when black bears are beefing up, often on trash, in Southern California’s foothill communities.
From fall to early winter, bears quadruple their food intake in preparation for the cooler months — bears here don’t really hibernate given our mild weather and plethora of resources, but they do slow down during the winter (as we all should). And right now, mother bears are looking to find a safe place to den and have their cubs.
Bears aren’t just roaming the roads of mountain towns either. They’re in suburban neighborhood streets along the 210 Freeway corridor — including Altadena, Sierra Madre and Monrovia — and even in Encino and Tarzana.
This time of year is when humans and bears might come into conflict more frequently, says a former biologist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
“You're going to see those bears just eating ravenously, foraging all day for food, and then also they're going to start looking for these potential denning sites under our crawl spaces, unfortunately,” said Jessica West, a human-wildlife conflict specialist who over the last five years worked for the state on bear coexistence efforts from Santa Barbara to San Diego.
Nearly 60,000 black bears are estimated to live in California. Here in Southern California, the estimate is around 2,000, according to the latest count by the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife.
Who's that bear?
Though they may appear brown or blond, black bears are the only species of bear in California.
For thousands of years, brown bears, also called grizzly bears, were the main bear of the California landscape, including here in Southern California. But European and American settlers killed them all off by the early 1900s.
Evidence of black bears in Southern California dates to about 25,000 years ago. The theory is they headed farther north in the middle of the Ice Age as the landscape here got a lot drier and the ancient forest disappeared.
So how did black bears come back? They were brought here by the government from Yosemite as a tourist attraction. (Wild right? If you want to dig deeper, listen to our podcast about black bears in Southern California.)
Black bears are omnivores and opportunists. They primarily eat plants and bugs, but they’ll also eat animal carcasses, small mammals and, of course, whatever’s in your trash.
State resources to help communities coexist with bears have been cut. That includes West, who was the sole wildlife conflict biologist serving Southern California counties. Gov. Gavin Newsom just signed a bill into law that aims to bring some of those resources back, but in the meantime, the need remains.
“More than ever, people and bears are sharing space,” West said. "The fact is that they're here and they're not going anywhere, and we're here as humans and we're not going anywhere.”
Neither did West’s passion for wildlife coexistence when she was laid off. That’s why she just launched her own business to help fill the resource gap: Wild Neighbor.
Jessica West, a bear biologist, installs an "unwelcome" mat at a home. The electrified mat helps keeps curious bears away.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
An "unwelcome" mat with bear prints outside of a home in Ojai.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
She offers detailed property assessments and recommendations for $150. She focuses primarily on prevention, such as strategically placing electric wiring and “unwelcome” mats to secure crawl spaces, trash and other vulnerable areas, which can cost $350 to around $900 depending on the home. She also rents such equipment if residents prefer. West works with manufacturers of electric bear-resistant tools that have been vetted for fire safety and bear conflict.
“What the science shows is that the most effective deterrent that we have at this point in time in our tool belt for bears is electricity,” West said. “There's really nothing like that in the wild for bears. It's a very novel stimulus for them.”
Don't attract bears
Get a bear-resistant trash can if your city offers it and it fits your budget. If you can’t, take your trash out as close to trash pickup as possible. (GPS collar data has shown that bears actually learn trash day schedules.) Or keep your trash inside a secure structure, like a closed garage.
Get rid of bird seed and hummingbird nectar feeders.
Bears have extremely powerful noses and can squeeze through even small opened windows to get to a refrigerator. So if bears are present in your neighborhood, keep accessible windows closed and locked as much as possible.
If a bear has already gotten into your crawl space, West can be hired to coax it out. But if a mother bear with cubs is under the house, West won’t evict them. Instead, she’ll work with the property owner to monitor the situation until the bear family leaves.
“We really want to avoid potentially orphaning those cubs,” she said.
It’s best to avoid allowing a bear to get into your crawl space or trash in the first place, West said. When bears become too accustomed to humans and eating human food, the risk of injury to people and pets rises. And the bears themselves are more likely to be euthanized.
In 2023, California hit a tragic milestone: It was the state’s first documented killing of a human by a black bear, in Northern California. In Southern California, foothill communities such as Sierra Madre have seen several bear-related injuries in recent years (more on that in our 2024 podcast on this topic). Several bears, including a well-known one in La Cañada Flintridge, have also been euthanized in recent years.
In the vast majority of cases, this is preventable, West said, if residents take a little responsibility for securing their own properties. That can also save thousands of dollars in damage caused by a bear.
Since West is no longer with the state, she can’t trap bears that have risen to the point of becoming a problem — for example, those that learn how to regularly get into homes or cars, or have lost their fear of humans. She does encourage her clients to share sightings and any concerning conflicts with the Department of Fish and Wildlife, but she doesn’t share anything herself without clients’ permission. (Learn how to report bear sightings or human-bear conflict here.)
West said that in lieu of state resources, companies like hers may become more common.
“What [clients] can expect is someone who is going to listen to them, and someone who is passionate about their job and really wants to help them,” West said. “Because at the end of the day, I'm a bear biologist by training. I love bears, but my whole goal in all of this is to help people. Because if we help people, we're also helping bears.”

Head outdoors
A number of listeners said hikes are their go-to cheap date.
“ I like going into an area where you get into a canopy, a lot of trees, so you don't get too warm,” Adrian in Corona said.
There might even be some science behind Angelenos’ love of hiking dates. Dating coach Damona Hoffman said there are benefits to doing something active while on a date.
“It boosts your endorphins… when you do something physical, you can sort of transfer some of those feelings of excitement to the person that you're with,” she said.
Kiz in Beverly Hills recommended Los Leones Canyon in Pacific Palisades — which is open after the Palisades fire — where he went on an early first date with his wife, adding that it’s also kid-friendly.
LAist host Austin Cross pointed out this may not be the best idea for a first date though.
“If the conversation's not hitting, but you're two miles into this hike, you still gotta walk back with them,” he said.
Take advantage of the arts
Heidi in Los Feliz recommended taking an art class, specifically at Heavy Manners Library in Echo Park.
“During the summer, the Hollywood Bowl has $6 seats for the symphony,” Adriana in Hollywood said. “You can take in your own food, you can bring in a bottle of wine, you can sit under the stars, listen to the LA Phil, and to me, that is just the most romantic, gorgeous way to spend a summer evening.”
Simplicity can be a good thing

“ It lends a lot to discussion of what you want in your future,” he said.

“Conversation came organically through looking at the type of books that we liked,” she said of her experience.
Cross used to go to IKEA on dates back in the day.
“It was also a fun cheap date because you could see a person in so many different settings,” he said. “You could see if they were game to pretend to play house.”
The beach triumphs as an all-time cheap date spot
Diane in West L.A. said — even after 41 years of marriage — eating dinner on the beach never fails.
“One of you can carry the basket, one of you can carry the blanket,” she said.

But tides were high earlier in the day and are expected to be over 7 feet this weekend. All the recent erosion, flooding and other damage raises questions about the long-term future of the peninsula.
The cooldown: Temperatures are expected to drop significantly over the weekend. By Monday, highs across L.A. and Orange counties will range from the mid-60s to the low 70s.

Topline:
With state resources having been cut, a former state biologist launches her own bear coexistence business.
Why it matters: It’s the time of year when black bears are beefing up — often on trash — in Southern California’s foothill communities. In recent years, these areas have seen a rise in conflicts with bears.
Read on ... for more on why one biologist who lost her job with the state is starting her own business to help communities live with bears.
It’s that time of year when black bears are beefing up, often on trash, in Southern California’s foothill communities.
From fall to early winter, bears quadruple their food intake in preparation for the cooler months — bears here don’t really hibernate given our mild weather and plethora of resources, but they do slow down during the winter (as we all should). And right now, mother bears are looking to find a safe place to den and have their cubs.
Bears aren’t just roaming the roads of mountain towns either. They’re in suburban neighborhood streets along the 210 Freeway corridor — including Altadena, Sierra Madre and Monrovia — and even in Encino and Tarzana.
This time of year is when humans and bears might come into conflict more frequently, says a former biologist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
“You're going to see those bears just eating ravenously, foraging all day for food, and then also they're going to start looking for these potential denning sites under our crawl spaces, unfortunately,” said Jessica West, a human-wildlife conflict specialist who over the last five years worked for the state on bear coexistence efforts from Santa Barbara to San Diego.
Nearly 60,000 black bears are estimated to live in California. Here in Southern California, the estimate is around 2,000, according to the latest count by the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife.
Who's that bear?
Though they may appear brown or blond, black bears are the only species of bear in California.
For thousands of years, brown bears, also called grizzly bears, were the main bear of the California landscape, including here in Southern California. But European and American settlers killed them all off by the early 1900s.
Evidence of black bears in Southern California dates to about 25,000 years ago. The theory is they headed farther north in the middle of the Ice Age as the landscape here got a lot drier and the ancient forest disappeared.
So how did black bears come back? They were brought here by the government from Yosemite as a tourist attraction. (Wild right? If you want to dig deeper, listen to our podcast about black bears in Southern California.)
Black bears are omnivores and opportunists. They primarily eat plants and bugs, but they’ll also eat animal carcasses, small mammals and, of course, whatever’s in your trash.
State resources to help communities coexist with bears have been cut. That includes West, who was the sole wildlife conflict biologist serving Southern California counties. Gov. Gavin Newsom just signed a bill into law that aims to bring some of those resources back, but in the meantime, the need remains.
“More than ever, people and bears are sharing space,” West said. "The fact is that they're here and they're not going anywhere, and we're here as humans and we're not going anywhere.”
Neither did West’s passion for wildlife coexistence when she was laid off. That’s why she just launched her own business to help fill the resource gap: Wild Neighbor.
Jessica West, a bear biologist, installs an "unwelcome" mat at a home. The electrified mat helps keeps curious bears away.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
An "unwelcome" mat with bear prints outside of a home in Ojai.
(
Courtesy Wild Neighbor
)
She offers detailed property assessments and recommendations for $150. She focuses primarily on prevention, such as strategically placing electric wiring and “unwelcome” mats to secure crawl spaces, trash and other vulnerable areas, which can cost $350 to around $900 depending on the home. She also rents such equipment if residents prefer. West works with manufacturers of electric bear-resistant tools that have been vetted for fire safety and bear conflict.
“What the science shows is that the most effective deterrent that we have at this point in time in our tool belt for bears is electricity,” West said. “There's really nothing like that in the wild for bears. It's a very novel stimulus for them.”
Don't attract bears
Get a bear-resistant trash can if your city offers it and it fits your budget. If you can’t, take your trash out as close to trash pickup as possible. (GPS collar data has shown that bears actually learn trash day schedules.) Or keep your trash inside a secure structure, like a closed garage.
Get rid of bird seed and hummingbird nectar feeders.
Bears have extremely powerful noses and can squeeze through even small opened windows to get to a refrigerator. So if bears are present in your neighborhood, keep accessible windows closed and locked as much as possible.
If a bear has already gotten into your crawl space, West can be hired to coax it out. But if a mother bear with cubs is under the house, West won’t evict them. Instead, she’ll work with the property owner to monitor the situation until the bear family leaves.
“We really want to avoid potentially orphaning those cubs,” she said.
It’s best to avoid allowing a bear to get into your crawl space or trash in the first place, West said. When bears become too accustomed to humans and eating human food, the risk of injury to people and pets rises. And the bears themselves are more likely to be euthanized.
In 2023, California hit a tragic milestone: It was the state’s first documented killing of a human by a black bear, in Northern California. In Southern California, foothill communities such as Sierra Madre have seen several bear-related injuries in recent years (more on that in our 2024 podcast on this topic). Several bears, including a well-known one in La Cañada Flintridge, have also been euthanized in recent years.
In the vast majority of cases, this is preventable, West said, if residents take a little responsibility for securing their own properties. That can also save thousands of dollars in damage caused by a bear.
Since West is no longer with the state, she can’t trap bears that have risen to the point of becoming a problem — for example, those that learn how to regularly get into homes or cars, or have lost their fear of humans. She does encourage her clients to share sightings and any concerning conflicts with the Department of Fish and Wildlife, but she doesn’t share anything herself without clients’ permission. (Learn how to report bear sightings or human-bear conflict here.)
West said that in lieu of state resources, companies like hers may become more common.
“What [clients] can expect is someone who is going to listen to them, and someone who is passionate about their job and really wants to help them,” West said. “Because at the end of the day, I'm a bear biologist by training. I love bears, but my whole goal in all of this is to help people. Because if we help people, we're also helping bears.”

title: From the coast to the backcountry , San Diego County sweats out a weekend heat wave
text:
Tom Foote slumped under a large umbrella at the Off Road Car Show at the Ramona Country Fair on Saturday. Even though it wasn’t yet noon, perspiration started bleeding through his khaki shirt.
“It’s pretty darn hot and I know I’m just going to get warmer,” the 77-year-old from Vista said, alluding to weather forecasts predicting a high in Ramona of 101 degrees.
The fair was one of multiple locations across San Diego County — from the beach to the backcountry — that left people and pets sweltering from a weekend heat wave powered by a high pressure system that sent temperatures soaring.
“This is definitely gonna be a hotter one for us,” said Kyle Dodson, one of the directors of the Ramona Chamber of Commerce, which organizes the fair.
The chamber posted tips, advising fair-goers to drink plenty of water, apply sunscreen, make sure to wear hats and seek shade between rides and shows.
In its 55th year, the fair runs through Sunday night. Despite the broiling conditions, officials expect attendance of about 3,000 to 4,000 each day.
“In the last couple years we’ve invested in big, massive 20-foot-by-40 foot canopies,” Dodson said, “and then we have designated cool zones that have a huge water-cooled fan.” Organizers have also installed an overhead misting system.
Kristin Olson of Lakeside protected her 7-week-old son Wyatt with a stroller equipped with a capacious shade that even had an electric fan directed at the infant’s face.
“We’re gonna stay right here under the shade and keep him hydrated. The misters work wonders,” Olson said, adding that she and her husband planned on staying only about one hour.
Hot weather blanketed virtually every segment of San Diego County.
Through 8 p.m. Sunday, the National Weather Service issued a heat advisory for coastal areas of San Diego County and an extreme heat warning for inland communities and valleys across the county, such as Escondido, El Cajon and Borrego Springs.
The heat wave descended in the midst of a busy summer entertainment weekend that lured thousands to venture outdoors.
The Padres, who consistently draw in excess of 42,000 fans per game, hosted the San Francisco Giants at Petco Park on Saturday evening. In Mission Valley, country singer Zach Bryan headlined the second night of his two-day outdoor concert at Snapdragon Stadium, drawing tens of thousands of fans.
At 3:15 p.m., San Diego Gas & Electric’s weather network showed readings of 101 degrees in Campo and Potrero and 112 degrees in Borrego.
Despite the hot spell, Dr. James N. Elia, facility medical director of the Sharp Grossmont Hospital Emergency Department, said as of mid-morning Saturday he and his colleagues had not seen an uptick in cases of heat exhaustion.
“My advice is to stay indoors when possible and if you’re going out, try to find shade as best you can,” Elia said. “One of the more important things is to stay hydrated.”
The Ramona Junior Fair runs parallel to the country fair and features young people showing off horses, livestock, goats and other animals.
“Mother Nature, she’s put cooler temperatures on backorder for us this weekend,” Junior Fair president Jeff Becker said.
He estimated the weather made Saturday’s event the hottest in about a decade, but swamp coolers, fans, misters and plenty of water in barns and pens offered critters much-needed relief.
“We take the health and safety of the animals very seriously, especially with the hot weather,” Becker said.
Just a few yards away, VooDoo, a 1,219-pound prize steer, happily gulped water from a trough. His owner, 19-year-old Josie Sand of the Ramona FFA, scheduled hydration breaks for VooDoo at least every half hour and sprayed water on his coat.
In an effort to blunt the effects of the heat, officials at the city of San Diego urged residents to take precautions.
“We encourage residents who need shelter from the heat to take advantage of one of our many sites available to cool down,” Office of Emergency Services Chief Rob Rezende said in a statement. “We also advise residents to check on elderly and vulnerable neighbors to make sure they are safe during this heat wave.”
The city designates selected recreation centers and libraries as places where the public and service animals can cool off when heat advisories are in effect. A list of the sites can found at www.sandiego.gov/PlacesToCoolDown.
In addition to the heat, lifeguards along the coast kept a sharp eye on beachgoers Saturday because of potentially dangerous rip currents, due to winds blowing from Hurricane Genevieve off the tip of Baja California.
Ocean temperatures have risen 3 to 7 degrees higher than normal, enticing people to take to the water, but big waves bolstered by Genevieve can pose a danger to swimmers.
In response, San Diego Fire-Rescue added about 20 more lifeguards to its regular full-capacity summer staff.
San Diego Lifeguard Chief James Gartland advises beachgoers to stay near lifeguard towers and check in with lifeguards to see what areas are best to swim and which spots to avoid.
“For us, the best rescue that we make is the one that doesn’t happen,” Gartland told the Union-Tribune on Friday.

title: A record - challenging heat dome is about to bake the West this weekend
text:
An unusually strong heat dome will scorch much of the western United States this weekend, bringing the hottest temperatures so far this year to tens of millions from California to Canada.
Dozens of record highs are expected to fall in at least 12 states in the West through the weekend with around 40 million people under heat alerts.
High temperatures will climb between 10 to nearly 20 degrees hotter than they should be — even for the peak of summer — from Southern California to the northern Rockies and Plains from Friday through Tuesday. Death Valley, California, is forecast to see the hottest temperature of this heat wave: a blistering 126 degrees.
RELATED STORY | What is a heat dome? Dangerous heat to grip central US
This is the latest in a spate of record-breaking heat waves that have affected the US and Europe simultaneously this summer. Human-caused climate change is making heat waves like this one more likely to occur, as well as more intense and longer-lasting, studies show. Particularly strong and slow-moving heat domes are also possibly becoming more common as the world warms, though this is an area of active research.
The heat dome responsible for this heat wave may also set records for its intensity in parts of Southern California and Arizona. Heat domes act like a lid on a pot, trapping and enhancing hot air beneath them. This one is expected to reach even higher in the atmosphere than typical, and that means it can trap even more air below it, raising the ceiling on just how extreme surface temperatures can get.
More than 12 million people across the Southwest, Mountain West and northern Great Plains are under a Level 4 of 4 “extreme” heat risk Saturday and Sunday, with an additional 12 million people under a Level 3 of 4 “major” heat risk. Heat at this level will affect anyone without access to cooling and hydration, the National Weather Service warns.
The weekend heat may just be the first wave of extreme temperatures from this heat dome as it settles in for the long haul, with more hot weather predicted in large parts of the West beginning on August 6.
Dangerous, record-setting heat
By August 4, around 10% of the continental US will record the hottest day of the year so far.
RELATED STORY | Record-breaking El Niño possible, bringing extreme weather, experts warn
Billings, Montana, is forecast to hit 106 degrees on Saturday, breaking its August record. The city recorded its hottest-ever temperature of 111 degrees just two weeks ago. Salt Lake City may set an August record with a forecast of 106 on Saturday, on the heels of breaking its all-time record high earlier this month.
In California, where highs across much of the state will reach 100 to 110 degrees, anyone seeking relief at the beaches will need to be cautious: Far offshore Hurricane Genevieve will send large waves and rip currents along the southern portion of the state. Lifeguards with the Los Angeles County Fire Department performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues last week as millions visited area beaches, the department said in a post on social media.
Phoenix and Tucson, Arizona, and Las Vegas are all expected to rise well above 110 degrees. In Maricopa County, home to Phoenix, there have been 40 confirmed heat-related deaths so far this year, county data shows, with months of summer heat still to come.
Heat is the deadliest type of extreme weather in the US, with a higher annual average death toll than tornadoes, hurricanes and lightning combined, National Weather Service statistics show. Emergency room visits for heat-related illness surge on “major” and “extreme” risk days, according to the weather service.
Overnight lows will also remain nearly 10 degrees above normal across the West, offering little relief even after dark. This lack of a cooldown is especially dangerous as it gives the body less time to recover before the next day’s heat builds again.
Heat triggers a wave of worrying impacts
The heat wave is also worsening wildfire and water concerns across the West, particularly the parched Colorado River Basin.
Much of the river basin as well as higher elevations in central and Southern California saw below average snowfall this past winter. This heat will dry out the ground further, making the region more vulnerable to wildfires.
RELATED STORY | Why floods are becoming more dangerous and what we can do to prevent them
Other concerns center on water and energy supplies, given the beleaguered state of the river basin.
The combined water level of Lake Mead and Lake Powell, two of the biggest US reservoirs, is at a historic low and continues to drop.
These reservoirs, together with the river basin overall, provide water to tens of millions of people. The heat wave will only exacerbate the rate of evaporation and decline in water levels from these critical resources.

title: Steady return to hot weather on tap for Bay Area
text:
A brief cool spell that sent temperatures below normal in the Bay Area is about to give way to conditions more common for late July, but the beach won’t be the safe retreat for relief that it might normally be.
The National Weather Service said temperatures will begin to elevate again on Monday, with the hottest inland areas such as Concord and Livermore forecast to move back into the low 90s. By the end of the week, the weather service anticipates temperatures will be above 95 degrees and threatening 100. In the Santa Clara Valley, the thermometer is expected to reach 90 by Friday.
Oakland is expected to be in the upper 70s all week, and San Francisco also is likely to see high temperatures in the 70s all week long.
All of which may drive people to consider a trip to the beach, an option that comes with considerable danger this week, the weather service said.
“We have two hurricanes in the eastern Pacific Ocean. The remnants of one of them — Hurricane Fausto — has been sending some strong swells to us,” NWS meteorologist Anamaria Navarrete said. “The swells have been over five feet and that’s caused some of the waves to be breaking at 10-11 feet. We also have Hurricane Genevieve that’s still far from us, so given what we’ve seen with the swells so far, that will probably continue. The sneaker waves and the rip tides are all that much stronger.”
Those conditions were caught on video at a Santa Cruz beach on video Sunday, where life guards and Good Samaritans helped to rescue a boy from powerful waves as they crashed over them.
A beach hazards statement issued by the weather service remained in effect Monday and will stay that way through Wednesday afternoon, though the weather service said that it’s possible it may last longer. Those at the beaches are expected to keep an eye on the waves and to stay off jetties, piers, rocks and other waterside infrastructure.
As for the increasing temperatures, those come courtesy the slight expansion of a heat dome that has enveloped much of the central and southern Plains, the southern Rockies, the Desert Southwest and the upper Midwest. In Death Valley, the high temperature forecast of 114 on Monday is expected to increase to 119 by Sunday.
A trough in the upper atmosphere along the Pacific Northwest has kept that dome away from the Bay Area until now. But the weather service said it is expanding and that the trough is shifting, causing temperatures to rise in the region.
“The dome is expanding westward,” Navarette said. “The trough is a bit more northward and not extending as far down and not as deep as it could be.”
The hot temperatures are expected to persist at least through the weekend, and temperatures may be forecast to be higher as the week progresses, depending on how much influence the heat dome is expected to wild.

title: Extreme heat warning remains in effect through at least Sunday
text:
San Diego officials are offering warnings and guidance for those headed out amid an extreme heat warning for all of Southern California this weekend.
Dangerously hot conditions with high temperatures in the mid-90s are forecast for San Diego’s western valleys, with temperatures climbing to around 105 near the foothills.
Temperatures ranging from mid-90s to mid-100s are also projected for mountain communities.
Meanwhile, desert communities could see temperatures rise to 115 or higher. Coastal areas will be cooler, but not by much, potentially hitting the mid-90s.
At the same time, the heat wave coincides with a coastal flood advisory due to large swells during high tide thanks to Hurricane Genevieve.
Genevieve’s southerly swell will continue to generate elevated surf through Friday before diminishing over the weekend. Sets up to nine feet will continue, with the highest on south-facing beaches.
“This will create conditions hazardous for inexperienced swimmers,” the National Weather Service’s San Diego office said in a forecast discussion, adding that high tides will exceed six feet each evening. “The combination of high tides and high surf increases the risk of coastal flooding.”
Those in coastal areas can expect “flooding of low-lying beach parking lots, boardwalks, and roads. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Breaking waves can sweep people off jetties and docks, and into dangerous seas,” the NWS added.
The city of San Diego designates recreation centers, libraries and other public buildings as places to seek relief from hot weather. Designated locations will be available during open hours; service animals will be allowed entry. Regularly scheduled programs and recreational activities may be taking place in these locations.
A full list of locations can be found here.
“We encourage residents who need shelter from the heat to take advantage of one of our many sites available to cool down,” said Office of Emergency Services chief Rob Rezende.
“We also advise residents to check on elderly and vulnerable neighbors to make sure they are safe during this heatwave.”
Three San Diego County parks are also closing for the month of August — an annual safety measure aimed at protecting residents during what is often the hottest time of the year.
El Capitan Preserve near Lakeside, Hellhole Canyon Preserve in Valley Center and Mt. Gower Preserve in Ramona will be closed through August. Agua Caliente Regional Park and Vallecito County Park, which are in or near the Anza- Borrego Desert, remain closed for the summer after shutting down Memorial Day weekend.
“Beyond heat-related safety, the seasonal closures allow Parks and Recreation to complete maintenance projects such as trail restoration,” the county added.
The parks will reopen Labor Day weekend.
Parks officials urge hikers to take extra precautions as dangerous health conditions persist.
San Diego’s park rangers encourage people to exercise caution if they choose to visit the city’s trails and parks and be prepared with proper attire and plenty of drinking water.
“It’s best to schedule hikes during the cooler morning or evening hours. Stay on the trails and leave pets at home during the heat of the day,” a city statement said.
The heat wave is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
City News Service contributed to this report.

title: Hurricane swell brings wild waves , challenging conditions for US Open of Surfing
text:
It was a constant battle with the ocean on the first full day of Challenger Series competition at the Lexus US Open of Surfing on Wednesday, July 29, with walls of wave after wave battering down on the competitors.
Strong, rushing rip currents tested competitors trying to survive their heats, with a safety team on watercraft ready to zip them back out to where the big waves were forming for their next rides.
It’s no typical year at the US Open of Surfing, with Hurricane Genevieve now bringing tricky, challenging, big-wave conditions to the Huntington Beach event. Waves in the 8- to 10-foot range crashed into whitewash, tickling the bottom of the famed pier on Wednesday where spectators lined up to cheer on the pro surfers.
Huntington Beach surfers fared well in the big waves, showing local knowledge paid off. Luke Guinaldo advanced in the men’s draw, and Bailey Turner on the women’s side, both bringing out big cheering sections on the sand.
Ahead of her heat, Turner studied the spitting barrels that were showing up, watching as waves jacked up to make a cave of water she was hoping to tuck into.
Turner had a tough start in her heat, she admitted, but in the second half was able to capitalize on several waves, pulling off big hacks and turns on beefy waves to earn a 5.77 and a 4.03 — enough to advance.
On her last wave, she made a huge turn and her body bent backward, engulfed in whitewash. She was able to pop back up, the crowd cheering, later joking that she had to really squeeze her abs to stand up on the board.
“I just needed a small score,” she said. “I just really needed to hang on.”
Turner grew up surfing the same spot with friends and family, “so it’s a dream just to go into the contest and just happy to surf heats,” she said.
Her dad, former pro surfer Ryan Turner, was among her fans on the beach cheering her on.
“So excited,” he said after she advanced. “I know how hard she works. She was waiting and wanted it to get bigger, she had some bigger boards… She has her plan.”
Huntington Beach High School surf coach Ian Dominelli said the 17-year-old, who recently won an ISA gold medal and took the win at the Jacks Surfboard Pro earlier this year, makes the surf town proud.
“She represents us,” he said. “She thrives when it’s big here, she’s always a standout.”
The coach knows the conditions are tricky, and only experience in these kinds of conditions — big, messy and wild — will help the athletes feel comfortable.
World Tour surfer and Canadian Erin Brooks, 19, is just off of a surf trip to Indonesia, where she got some experience with big waves that helped her prepare for what the ocean was throwing at the US Open competitors, she said.
She earned a high 8.33 and backed it up with a 5.67 to take the first spot in the same heat with Turner on Wednesday.
“I’ve never seen Huntington this size,” she said. “I got a lot of practice in big waves, so I felt super, super comfortable.”
The day was all about big turns and the competitors finding critical sections to dig their rails into — the surf was too wild and messy to try to pull off big airs, even for skilled aerialists like Brooks.
Encinitas surfer Alyssa Spencer found a few gems among the chaos in the water.
“It’s definitely a lot different than we usually see in Huntington Beach, it’s not every day we see a huge hurricane swell that comes through, but there’s a couple really good waves out there amongst the challenging water moving and current and everything else going on,” she said. “It’s definitely really exciting, that’s for sure.”
Though she also surfs on the elite World Tour, the US Open is the big, prestigious event for California, Spencer said, and a win would “mean everything.”
“That’s a big reason I’m here doing it, it’s a big goal for me and I’m hoping to make it happen this year,” she said.
French surfer Johanne Defay put the jersey back on for the first time since having her baby, now 11 months old, thinking Huntington Beach would be a good place to ease back into competition.
“For Huntington Beach, I wasn’t expecting this,” she said after advancing in her heat. “I chose the US Open to start in smaller waves, but that’s what surfing is all about. It’s always different and surprising.”
San Clemente surfer Eden Walla, 16, hunted for left-handers that were reeling from the south end of the contest area, rather than staying by the pier where surfers earlier in the day were getting stuck in rip currents near the concrete pylons. When the heat started, she paddled out three lifeguard towers down the beach, but the current quickly moved her north toward the pier.
It was Walla’s first time using a jet ski assist in a contest.
“It’s never been big enough in any contest I’ve been in,” she said. “It was super nice to be able to use them… I probably would have caught two waves in that heat if we didn’t have the jet ski. It makes it so everyone can surf more, and do less paddling.”
The big waves in the contest made for an exciting day for both surfers and spectators, she said.
“I think it makes it way more entertaining for everyone on the beach. It is super nice to have bigger waves, and not have to worry if the waves may not come,” she said. “There’s always going to be some waves coming.”
The men’s action got underway by the afternoon, the lower-seeded competitors needing to scrap through more heats to make it to finals day.
In the Round of 80, the top two surfers get a chance to gain momentum and confidence before they move to the next round and face higher-level competition against others hoping to earn valuable Challenger Series points, as well as some of the world’s best surfers already at the elite level.
For the bottom two in the heats who can’t find the score they need, they must pack their bags and start thinking about the next event.

title: Trump invites teen lifeguard to White House following rescue at California beach
text:
President Donald Trump said he wants to invite the teenage lifeguard who rescued a 10-year-old child from the pounding surf at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz Saturday to the White House and honor him.
“We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor,” Trump wrote in a social media post. “Very brave, he deserves it!”
At approximately 3:32 p.m. Saturday on the beach area across from the corner of Mott Avenue and East Cliff Drive, the 16-year-old California State Parks lifeguard was conducting a routine safety check on the shore with another visitor when he spotted a child out in the water. According to State Parks Operations Superintendent Scott Sipes, the child had been knocked down by a crashing wave and was quickly swept out about 15 yards offshore by the powerful current.
Video of the harrowing incident, captured by photographer Scott Vander Dussen and posted to his Instagram account “santacruznow,” begins with the lifeguard clutching the child in waist-high whitewash before a wall of water rushes through the frame as the pair attempts to duck underneath. Sipes said the waves were approximately 8 feet tall and were generated by Hurricane Genevieve, a Category 4 hurricane in the Pacific Ocean near Mexico.
The lifeguard, whose identity is being withheld due to his status as a minor, attempted to pull the child to shore as the water rushed back out to sea, and though he makes some progress, there’s not enough time between wave intervals to reach the dry sand as the cycle of attempting to take cover beneath the heavy shore break continued. Several bystanders entered the water in an attempt to assist with the rescue, but some of them were also inundated by the huge waves and rapid current and were nearly swept out as well, according to the video, which has attracted attention from news outlets across the country.
Eventually, a second lifeguard arrived at the scene and assisted with extracting the child from the water. The child, apparently exhausted and unable to stand, according to the video, was unharmed and was reunited with their mother. Sipes said the teenage lifeguard, healthy and in high spirits after the rescue, clocked back in for another shift Sunday.
Sipes added that the incident Saturday was one of 34 rescues that were performed by local lifeguards in Santa Cruz County over the weekend.
“It’s not always immediately apparent that there is this significant risk because there can be a delay between the intervals of wave sets,” said Sipes. “So conditions could, theoretically, look calm for a moment until another set arrives. And because of the energy and the size of the waves, it can be so detrimental that it would catch an unassuming swimmer by surprise.”
Sipes also said the rescue was a reminder to other members of the public that, unless they are professionally trained, they should remain on the beach and call in for other authorities if they see someone in distress. Otherwise, the bystanders could complicate the effort and require rescuing of their own.
“Sometimes, well-intended people can become overwhelmed themselves and actually add to the rescue,” added Sipes. “We were very fortunate they all made it out.”
Sipes stressed that the dangerous coastal conditions are expected to last at least through Thursday and said members of the public can stay safe by checking in with a lifeguard before entering the water and never turning their back on the ocean.
The National Weather Service has included the county in a beach hazards statement that will last through 5 p.m. Saturday. Breaking waves could reach up to 10 feet tall with sneaker waves and strong rip currents expected to continue to occur as well.

title: A record - challenging heat dome is about to bake the West this weekend
text:
An unusually strong heat dome will scorch much of the western United States this weekend, bringing the hottest temperatures so far this year to tens of millions from California to Canada.
Dozens of record highs are expected to fall in at least 12 states in the West through the weekend with around 40 million people under heat alerts.
High temperatures will climb between 10 to nearly 20 degrees hotter than they should be — even for the peak of summer — from Southern California to the northern Rockies and Plains from Friday through Tuesday. Death Valley, California, is forecast to see the hottest temperature of this heat wave: a blistering 126 degrees.
RELATED STORY | What is a heat dome? Dangerous heat to grip central US
This is the latest in a spate of record-breaking heat waves that have affected the US and Europe simultaneously this summer. Human-caused climate change is making heat waves like this one more likely to occur, as well as more intense and longer-lasting, studies show. Particularly strong and slow-moving heat domes are also possibly becoming more common as the world warms, though this is an area of active research.
The heat dome responsible for this heat wave may also set records for its intensity in parts of Southern California and Arizona. Heat domes act like a lid on a pot, trapping and enhancing hot air beneath them. This one is expected to reach even higher in the atmosphere than typical, and that means it can trap even more air below it, raising the ceiling on just how extreme surface temperatures can get.
More than 12 million people across the Southwest, Mountain West and northern Great Plains are under a Level 4 of 4 “extreme” heat risk Saturday and Sunday, with an additional 12 million people under a Level 3 of 4 “major” heat risk. Heat at this level will affect anyone without access to cooling and hydration, the National Weather Service warns.
The weekend heat may just be the first wave of extreme temperatures from this heat dome as it settles in for the long haul, with more hot weather predicted in large parts of the West beginning on August 6.
Dangerous, record-setting heat
By August 4, around 10% of the continental US will record the hottest day of the year so far.
RELATED STORY | Record-breaking El Niño possible, bringing extreme weather, experts warn
Billings, Montana, is forecast to hit 106 degrees on Saturday, breaking its August record. The city recorded its hottest-ever temperature of 111 degrees just two weeks ago. Salt Lake City may set an August record with a forecast of 106 on Saturday, on the heels of breaking its all-time record high earlier this month.
In California, where highs across much of the state will reach 100 to 110 degrees, anyone seeking relief at the beaches will need to be cautious: Far offshore Hurricane Genevieve will send large waves and rip currents along the southern portion of the state. Lifeguards with the Los Angeles County Fire Department performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues last week as millions visited area beaches, the department said in a post on social media.
Phoenix and Tucson, Arizona, and Las Vegas are all expected to rise well above 110 degrees. In Maricopa County, home to Phoenix, there have been 40 confirmed heat-related deaths so far this year, county data shows, with months of summer heat still to come.
Heat is the deadliest type of extreme weather in the US, with a higher annual average death toll than tornadoes, hurricanes and lightning combined, National Weather Service statistics show. Emergency room visits for heat-related illness surge on “major” and “extreme” risk days, according to the weather service.
Overnight lows will also remain nearly 10 degrees above normal across the West, offering little relief even after dark. This lack of a cooldown is especially dangerous as it gives the body less time to recover before the next day’s heat builds again.
Heat triggers a wave of worrying impacts
The heat wave is also worsening wildfire and water concerns across the West, particularly the parched Colorado River Basin.
Much of the river basin as well as higher elevations in central and Southern California saw below average snowfall this past winter. This heat will dry out the ground further, making the region more vulnerable to wildfires.
RELATED STORY | Why floods are becoming more dangerous and what we can do to prevent them
Other concerns center on water and energy supplies, given the beleaguered state of the river basin.
The combined water level of Lake Mead and Lake Powell, two of the biggest US reservoirs, is at a historic low and continues to drop.
These reservoirs, together with the river basin overall, provide water to tens of millions of people. The heat wave will only exacerbate the rate of evaporation and decline in water levels from these critical resources.
